name: Pectoralis Major
landmarks: Lateral third of Clavicle (palpate along the clavicle from the sternum laterally — the lateral third is roughly where the deltopectoral groove begins)
Coracoid Process (palpate below the lateral clavicle — feel for a bony bump under the anterior deltoid by pressing posteriorly into the deltopectoral triangle)
Sternal Border (palpate the lateral edge of the sternum — the pectoralis major attaches along this bony ridge)
Anterior axillary fold — the muscle itself forms this fold. Palpate with the arm abducted to 45-90°.
Sternocostal border (lower) and clavicular border (upper) define different fiber groups — the injection site sits inside the fold the muscle creates.
placement: Position the patient supine with the arm abducted 30-45 degrees and externally rotated slightly to open the chest.
Identify the lateral third of the clavicle by palpating from the sternoclavicular joint laterally.
For the clavicular head: insert the needle 2-3 cm inferior to the lateral clavicle, angled slightly caudally at about 30 degrees to the skin surface.
Advance the needle 1-2 cm into the muscle belly — you should feel the firm resistance of muscle tissue.
For the sternal head: palpate the bulk of the muscle mid-chest, approximately 3-4 cm lateral to the sternal border at the level of the 3rd-4th rib.

Insert the needle TANGENTIALLY to the chest wall (15-30° from the skin, NEVER perpendicular) and aim the needle path OVER a rib, never over an intercostal space. The rib acts as a hard backstop and protects against pleural puncture.
Under ultrasound, confirm the needle tip is in pec major and the rib's bright cortical line is directly deep to the needle path before injecting.
Aspirate before injecting to confirm you are not intravascular. Distribute the dose across 2-3 sites in the muscle belly.
Injection site: within the anterior axillary fold.
Direction: medially, along the fiber course.
setup: Ultrasound (USG) is highly recommended for this injection.
Visualize the Pectoralis Major overlying the Pectoralis Minor — the injection target is the superficial muscle belly only.
Use a high-frequency linear probe placed transversely across the chest wall to identify the two layers.
Avoid the rib interspaces to prevent pneumothorax — always confirm needle depth with ultrasound.
Patient position: sitting or supine, with the arm abducted to approximately 45-90°.
Attention: vessels and nerves run cranial (above) the muscle — stay below the axillary neurovascular bundle.

ultrasound.probe: High-frequency linear (10-15 MHz), Samsung LA3-16AD recommended
ultrasound.orientation: Transverse across the anterior chest wall, lateral to the sternal border at the 3rd-4th rib level
viewSteps: Position the patient supine with the arm slightly abducted. Place the probe transversely on the anterior chest.
The Pectoralis Major appears as the broad, flat superficial muscle layer directly under the subcutaneous fat — it spans most of the anterior chest.
Deep to the Pectoralis Major, a thin hyperechoic fascial plane separates it from the Pectoralis Minor.
The Pectoralis Minor appears as a smaller triangular muscle deep to the fascial plane.

CRITICAL: The Medial Pectoral Nerve (from the medial cord — confusingly named) passes through or between Pectoralis Major and Minor in the inter-fascial plane. The Lateral Pectoral Nerve (from the lateral cord) pierces the clavipectoral fascia to reach Pec Major directly. Both may be visible as hyperechoic dots with adjacent vessels.
Deep to Pectoralis Minor, the hyperechoic pleural line and ribs are visible — the lung appears as a bright sliding line with comet-tail artifacts.
Confirm by having the patient adduct the arm against resistance — Pec Major will contract.
safetyNotes: PNEUMOTHORAX RISK: The lung lies deep to the pectoralis muscles, separated only by a thin layer of intercostal muscle in the spaces between ribs. NEVER use a perpendicular needle approach. Always angle the needle tangentially to the chest wall and aim the trajectory OVER a rib (which acts as a backstop), never over an intercostal space.

The brachial plexus and axillary vessels run in the axilla just lateral to pec major — do not let the needle drift laterally into the axillary fossa. Use color Doppler to map the axillary artery before injection.
The Lateral Pectoral Nerve runs between Pec Major and Minor — avoid the inter-fascial plane.
Use real-time US guidance to keep the needle within the Pec Major muscle belly at all times.
The thoracoacromial artery runs in the deltopectoral groove — use color Doppler laterally.
ultrasound.videoSource: Dr. Andrei Bursuc — Pectoralis Major and Minor spasticity (Annotated US)

probePlacementHint: Patient supine, arm abducted 30°. Place probe transversely on anterior chest, lateral to sternum at 3rd-4th rib. Photo from patient's right side showing probe on chest wall.
pearls: Use 25-50U Botox per injection site, distributed across 2-3 sites per head, for a total session dose as listed in the dosage field.
A spastic pec major is the #1 cause of shoulder internal rotation/adduction posture
The sternocostal fibers form the anterior border of the axilla; the clavicular fibers define the border of the infraclavicular fossa.
Can function as an accessory muscle of inspiration; the sternocostal fibers are important when walking on crutches.
supplies: 25-27G needle (1.5 inch for superficial, 2-3 inch for deep)
dosageNote: Total across both heads. Split dose between clavicular and sternal heads (e.g. 25-50U each).
dangerZones: Avoid injecting too medially near the sternum to prevent spread to intercostals
positionLabel: Supine · arm abducted, externally rotated

name: Latissimus Dorsi
landmarks: Inferior Angle of Scapula (palpate the lowest bony point of the scapula with the patient's arm at the side — the lat dorsi wraps around just below here)
Posterior Axillary Fold (grasp the fold of skin/muscle behind the armpit — the latissimus dorsi forms this fold)
Iliac Crest (palpate the superior rim of the pelvis posterolaterally — the muscle originates broadly from this structure)
Inferior angle of the scapula — the muscle wraps around and below this.
Posterior axillary fold — latissimus forms its lower border.
placement: Position the patient in lateral decubitus with the affected side up, or prone with arm slightly abducted.
Grasp the posterior axillary fold between your thumb and fingers to identify the muscle bulk.
Palpate the Latissimus Dorsi — it is the lateral and superficial muscle forming the fold (Teres Major is deeper and more superior).
Identify the injection site approximately 4-5 cm inferior to the axillary crease along the mid-axillary line.
Insert the needle perpendicular to the skin into the mid-belly of the muscle.
Advance 1-2 cm into the muscle substance; you should feel firm muscular resistance.
Aspirate before injecting. Distribute the total dose across 2-3 sites along the muscle belly.
Target the muscle belly 7-8 cm lateral to the spine, at or below the scapular tip level.
setup: USG is helpful to distinguish Latissimus Dorsi from Teres Major and Serratus Anterior.
Patient positioning in lateral decubitus with affected side up provides the best access.
Have the patient adduct the arm against resistance to confirm palpation of the correct muscle.
The muscle becomes tendinous as it approaches the intertubercular groove — inject into the fleshy belly, not the tendon.
Patient position: prone with the arm flexed at the shoulder (overhead) to spread the muscle.

ultrasound.orientation: Transverse across the posterior axillary fold, perpendicular to the long axis of the muscle fibers
viewSteps: Identify subcutaneous tissue superficially as a hyperechoic layer.
The Latissimus Dorsi appears as a broad, flat hypoechoic muscle with a bright fascial envelope — it is the most superficial muscle in the posterior axillary fold.
Deep to the Latissimus Dorsi, identify the Teres Major as a separate hypoechoic muscle belly separated by a fascial plane.
Further deep and anteriorly, the Serratus Anterior may be seen as thin hypoechoic slips overlying the ribs.
safetyNotes: The thoracodorsal nerve and artery run along the deep surface of the Latissimus Dorsi — use color Doppler to identify the vascular bundle.
Avoid the axillary neurovascular bundle by staying inferior and posterior to the axillary crease.
The long thoracic nerve runs along the Serratus Anterior — do not inject too deep.
ultrasound.videoSource: Dr. Andrei Bursuc - Latissimus dorsi (spasticity)

probePlacementHint: Patient lateral decubitus or prone. Place probe transversely across posterior axillary fold. Photo from behind showing probe on lateral back/axilla.
pearls: Often co-injected with pec major and teres major for shoulder adduction/IR pattern
The posterior axillary fold is your best landmark — inject into the muscle belly as it crosses the fold
Lat dorsi contribution to spasticity is underappreciated — always assess it in shoulder posturing
Action is very similar to teres major — consider them together; palpation cannot always distinguish them.
supplies: 25-27G needle (1.5 inch for superficial, 2-3 inch for deep)
dosageNote: Large muscle — distribute across 2-3 sites along the posterior axillary fold.
dangerZones: The thoracodorsal nerve and artery run along the deep surface of the Latissimus Dorsi — use color Doppler to identify the vascular bundle.
Avoid the axillary neurovascular bundle by staying inferior and posterior to the axillary crease.
The long thoracic nerve runs along the Serratus Anterior — do not inject too deep.
positionLabel: Lateral decubitus (or prone) · arm slightly abducted

name: Teres Major
landmarks: Inferior Angle of the Scapula (palpate the lowest point of the scapula posteriorly — ask the patient to retract the scapula to make it prominent; the teres major originates from the posterior surface near the inferior angle and the lower lateral border)

Posterior Axillary Fold (grasp the fold of tissue at the back of the axilla — the teres major and latissimus dorsi form this fold; the teres major is the more superior and lateral of the two muscles in this fold)

Intertubercular (Bicipital) Groove of the Humerus (palpate the anterior shoulder between the greater and lesser tuberosities — the teres major inserts on the medial lip of the bicipital groove, along with the latissimus dorsi)
Inferior angle of the scapula (origin) — palpate the bony corner.
Posterior axillary fold — teres major contributes to it along with latissimus dorsi.
placement: Position the patient seated or prone with the arm adducted at the side.
Identify the posterior axillary fold and the inferior angle of the scapula.

Palpate the teres major — ask the patient to internally rotate and adduct the arm against resistance; the teres major contracts in the posterior axillary fold, superior and lateral to the latissimus dorsi.
The teres major lies along the lateral border of the scapula, running from the inferior angle to the humerus.
Insert the needle into the bulk of the muscle belly at the level of the inferior scapular angle, approximately 2-3 cm lateral to the lateral border of the scapula.
Advance 1.5-2 cm perpendicular to the skin.
Distinguish from the latissimus dorsi, which wraps around the teres major inferiorly — the teres major has a rounder, shorter belly.
Aspirate before injecting.
Injection site: into the muscle belly along the lateral border of the scapula, below the level of the infraspinatus.
setup: USG is recommended to distinguish teres major from the latissimus dorsi and teres minor, which are in close proximity.
Have the patient internally rotate the arm against resistance to identify the muscle belly in the posterior axillary fold.
The latissimus dorsi wraps around and lies superficial to the teres major at the posterior axillary fold — ultrasound helps separate the two.
The circumflex scapular artery passes through the triangular space (bordered by teres minor, teres major, and long head of triceps) — identify this with Doppler.
Patient position: prone or lateral decubitus, arm in neutral.

ultrasound.probe: High-frequency linear (10-15 MHz) or curvilinear for deeper patients
ultrasound.orientation: Transverse (short-axis) over the posterior axillary fold, with the patient's arm slightly abducted
viewSteps: Position the patient seated or prone with the arm slightly abducted. Place the probe on the posterior axillary fold.
The Teres Major appears as a flat, broad hypoechoic muscle at the inferior aspect of the posterior axillary fold — in Dr. Bursuc's video it is highlighted with a purple overlay.
The Latissimus Dorsi tendon wraps around and interdigitates with the Teres Major at this level — they may appear as adjacent muscle layers.
Deep to these muscles, the scapular bone and infraspinous fossa may be partially visible.
To confirm: ask the patient to internally rotate and adduct the arm against resistance — the Teres Major will contract.
Note: the video annotation labels 'LAT D' (Latissimus Dorsi) adjacent to the Teres Major.
safetyNotes: The circumflex scapular artery and thoracodorsal neurovascular bundle run near the Teres Major — use color Doppler.
The axillary nerve is superior to the Teres Major — avoid angling the needle superiorly.
The long head of the triceps is adjacent inferiorly — confirm your target with dynamic scanning.
ultrasound.videoSource: Dr. Andrei Bursuc — Teres Major Spasticity (Annotated US)

probePlacementHint: Patient seated or prone, arm at side. Place probe transversely over posterior axillary fold. Photo from behind showing probe on posterior axilla/inferior scapular angle.
pearls: Works synergistically with lat dorsi and subscapularis for shoulder IR/adduction
Often the forgotten muscle in shoulder internal rotation pattern — always assess it
The posterior axillary fold contains both lat dorsi and teres major — differentiate on US
Palpation can be challenging due to overlying latissimus — the two muscles are often fused and have very similar action.
Consider together with latissimus dorsi in adduction / internal-rotation spasticity.
supplies: 25-27G needle (1.5 inch for superficial, 2-3 inch for deep)
dosageNote: Large rotator. Distribute across 1-2 sites.
dangerZones: The circumflex scapular artery and thoracodorsal neurovascular bundle run near the Teres Major — use color Doppler.
The axillary nerve is superior to the Teres Major — avoid angling the needle superiorly.
positionLabel: Seated or prone · arm adducted at the side

name: Biceps Brachii
landmarks: Coracoid Process (palpate below the lateral clavicle — feel for a bony prominence deep to the anterior deltoid; the short head originates here)
Acromion (palpate the bony shelf at the top of the shoulder — follow the spine of the scapula laterally to its tip)
Cubital Fossa (the triangular depression on the anterior elbow — bounded by brachioradialis laterally and pronator teres medially)
Mid-humeral level on the anterior arm — halfway between the coracoid process and the cubital fossa.
placement: Position the patient supine or seated with the arm supinated and elbow extended, resting on a support surface.
Identify the mid-point of the humerus on the anterior arm (halfway between the acromion and lateral epicondyle).
Palpate the biceps muscle belly — ask the patient to flex the elbow slightly against resistance to confirm.
Insert the needle into the bulk of the muscle belly at the mid-humeral level, perpendicular to the skin surface.
Advance 1-1.5 cm into the muscle — the biceps is a superficial muscle, so you do not need to go deep.
Stay superficial to the Brachialis muscle (which lies deep against the humerus).
Aspirate before injecting. You may inject both the long and short heads if needed, spacing injections 2-3 cm apart.
Standard sites: 2-4 across the muscle belly for typical dosing.
setup: Surface anatomy is usually sufficient for this injection given the prominent muscle belly.
USG confirms depth to avoid the brachial neurovascular bundle, which runs medially in the arm.
Have the patient flex the elbow against resistance to identify the muscle belly before marking.
The musculocutaneous nerve enters the muscle from the lateral side — stay in the central belly.

ultrasound.orientation: Transverse (short-axis) over the anterior arm at the mid-humeral level
viewSteps: Position the patient supine with the arm slightly abducted and externally rotated. Place the probe transversely on the anterior arm.
The Biceps Brachii (short and long heads) appears as the large superficial hypoechoic muscle — it is the most prominent structure in the anterior compartment.
CRITICAL: The Musculocutaneous Nerve appears as a small hyperechoic oval within or at the deep border of the biceps — it typically sits between the biceps and brachialis muscles.
Deep to the biceps, the Brachialis muscle wraps around the anterior humerus.
The Radial Nerve may be visible laterally in the deeper plane, between the brachialis and the lateral intermuscular septum.
To distinguish short from long head: the short head is medial, the long head is lateral — a fascial septum often separates them.
safetyNotes: The Musculocutaneous Nerve runs between the biceps and brachialis — inject into the superficial belly of the biceps only.
The brachial artery and vein run on the medial side of the arm — avoid the medial approach.
The median nerve also runs medially — use an anterior or lateral approach for safety.
ultrasound.videoSource: Dr. Andrei Bursuc — Short head of biceps spasticity (Annotated US)

probePlacementHint: Patient supine, arm supinated. Place probe transversely on anterior mid-upper arm. Photo from lateral view showing probe across biceps belly.
pearls: One of the most commonly injected muscles in upper limb spasticity
Differentiate from brachialis — biceps is superficial and has a characteristic double-belly on US
If elbow flexion persists after biceps injection, the brachialis is likely the bigger contributor
Biceps is usually treated together with brachialis and brachioradialis — all three elbow flexors are viewed in synergy.
When treating elbow-flexion spasticity, consider distributing dose across biceps, brachialis, and brachioradialis rather than concentrating in biceps alone — the three work as a functional group.
supplies: 25-27G needle (1.5 inch for superficial, 2-3 inch for deep)
dosageNote: Large muscle with 2 heads. Split across short and long heads. FDA PI allows up to 200 U.
dangerZones: The Musculocutaneous Nerve runs between the biceps and brachialis — inject into the superficial belly of the biceps only.
The brachial artery and vein run on the medial side of the arm — avoid the medial approach.
The median nerve also runs medially — use an anterior or lateral approach for safety.
positionLabel: Supine or seated · arm supinated on a support

name: Brachialis
landmarks: Distal Humerus (palpate the anterior arm distally — feel the bony shaft of the humerus just proximal to the elbow)
Biceps Tendon (palpate the firm cord in the antecubital fossa during resisted flexion — the brachialis lies deep to this)
Lateral Epicondyle (palpate the bony prominence on the lateral elbow — the brachialis inserts on the coronoid process just proximal to this level)
Elbow fold — measure 3-4 cm proximal to it for the injection site.
Biceps tendon — the brachialis lies lateral and deep to it.
placement: Position the patient supine or seated with the elbow slightly flexed (about 30 degrees) and the forearm supinated.

Use an ANTERIOR approach through the biceps muscle belly in the distal third of the arm — this avoids both the medial neurovascular bundle and the radial nerve, which dives around the lateral humerus into the spiral groove.
Palpate the biceps muscle belly in the distal third of the arm (about 4-6 cm proximal to the elbow crease).
Under ultrasound, identify biceps as the superficial muscle and brachialis as the deeper hypoechoic muscle directly on the humeral cortex.
Insert the needle perpendicular to the skin through the biceps belly, advancing into the brachialis below it.
Confirm the needle tip is in brachialis (deep) and not biceps (superficial) before injecting.
Stop advancing just before contacting bone — the target is the muscle belly, not the periosteum.
Aspirate before injecting to rule out intravascular placement.
Injection site: approximately 3-4 cm proximal to the elbow fold, lateral to the biceps tendon, into the belly of brachialis deep to the biceps.
Sites: 1-2 per treatment.
setup: USG is MANDATORY for brachialis injection — the radial nerve courses around the lateral humerus and is at risk with any lateral approach.
Use an anterior in-plane approach through biceps. The needle should be visible on US the entire time.
Ensure the needle tip is in the muscular plane deep to the biceps but superficial to the humerus.
The brachial artery and median nerve lie medial — keep the needle in the central/anterior plane.
Consider EMG guidance as an adjunct to confirm placement in the correct muscle.

ultrasound.orientation: Transverse across the anterior distal third of the arm, ~4-6 cm proximal to the elbow crease (matching the anterior-through-biceps approach)
viewSteps: Place the probe transversely across the anterior distal third of the arm, ~4-6 cm proximal to the elbow crease.
Identify subcutaneous tissue and the superficial hyperechoic fascia.
The Biceps Brachii is visible as a superficial oval hypoechoic muscle belly with a central tendon distally.
Deep to the Biceps, the Brachialis appears as a flattened hypoechoic muscle directly against the hyperechoic cortex of the distal humerus.
The bright cortical line of the humerus serves as your deep landmark — stop the needle before reaching it.
Scan laterally to identify the radial nerve in the spiral groove (small hyperechoic honeycomb) so you know where it is — your anterior approach should keep you well away from it.
safetyNotes: The radial nerve courses along the lateral and posterior humerus in the spiral groove — always identify it before needle insertion.

The brachial artery and median nerve lie medially — the ANTERIOR approach through the biceps (as described in placement) keeps the needle medial to the radial nerve and lateral to the brachial vessels, providing the safest corridor.
Avoid contacting the periosteum of the humerus, which can cause significant pain.

probePlacementHint: Patient supine, elbow slightly flexed. Place probe transversely on anterior distal arm, 4-6 cm above elbow crease. Photo showing probe on anterior distal arm.
pearls: Often the primary elbow flexor in spasticity — don't skip it just because biceps is more famous
Lies deep to the biceps — must see both muscles on US to inject the correct one
Higher doses often needed here vs biceps since brachialis is the primary elbow flexor

Brachialis is often under-treated in elbow-flexor spasticity; it contributes substantial force to elbow flexion and is worth including when planning the distribution of dose across the elbow-flexor group.
Treat brachialis in cases of elbow-flexor spasticity; the dose is distributed among all elbow flexors rather than concentrated in biceps.
supplies: 25-27G needle (1.5 inch for superficial, 2-3 inch for deep)
dosageNote: Deep to biceps — often underdosed. Confirm placement on US before injecting.
anatomyCaption: Anterior arm · brachialis highlighted (deep to biceps)
dangerZones: The radial nerve courses along the lateral and posterior humerus in the spiral groove — always identify it before needle insertion.

The brachial artery and median nerve lie medially — the ANTERIOR approach through the biceps (as described in placement) keeps the needle medial to the radial nerve and lateral to the brachial vessels, providing the safest corridor.
Avoid contacting the periosteum of the humerus, which can cause significant pain.
positionLabel: Supine or seated · arm supinated on a support

name: Triceps
landmarks: Acromion (palpate the bony shelf at the tip of the shoulder — follow the spine of the scapula laterally to its most lateral point)
Olecranon (palpate the prominent bony point at the posterior elbow — this is the insertion of the triceps tendon)
Posterior Midline of Humerus (draw an imaginary line from the acromion to the olecranon along the posterior arm — the muscle belly is centered here)
Center of each muscle belly (long head, lateral head, medial head) — each head is treated as an independent belly.
placement: Position the patient seated or prone with the arm resting on a support, elbow flexed to approximately 90 degrees.
Identify the posterior midpoint of the humerus (halfway between the acromion and the olecranon).
Palpate the triceps muscle belly — ask the patient to extend the elbow against resistance to confirm the bulk of the long and lateral heads.
For the long head: insert the needle into the medial portion of the posterior arm at mid-humeral level, perpendicular to the skin.
For the lateral head: insert the needle into the lateral portion of the posterior arm, slightly more proximal, perpendicular to the skin.
Advance 1.5-2 cm into the muscle belly — the triceps is a large, superficial muscle on the posterior arm.
Avoid the medial aspect of the distal arm where the ulnar nerve courses in the ulnar groove behind the medial epicondyle.
Aspirate before injecting. Distribute injections across both heads if needed, spacing sites 3-4 cm apart.
Sites: 3-4 total, depending on dose and indication (typically 3 for routine spasticity).
Direction: vertical, or along the fiber course.
Injection depth: dictated by the thickness of the targeted head — thinner distally, thicker proximally.
When injecting the lateral head, confirm it is distinguishable from the overlying deltoid.
setup: Surface anatomy is usually adequate given the large, easily palpable muscle belly.
USG can help distinguish the long head from the lateral head and confirm depth.
Have the patient extend the elbow against resistance to identify and mark the muscle belly before injection.
The radial nerve courses in the spiral groove of the humerus on the posterolateral aspect — stay in the central or medial muscle belly at the mid-humeral level to avoid it.
Patient position: sitting or prone, with the shoulder slightly abducted.

ultrasound.orientation: Transverse (short-axis) over the posterior arm at the mid-humeral level
viewSteps: Position the patient prone or seated with the arm supported. Place the probe transversely on the posterior arm.
The Long Head of the Triceps appears as the large, prominent hypoechoic muscle — it is the most superficial and medial of the three triceps heads at the mid-arm level.
The humerus appears as a bright curved hyperechoic line with posterior acoustic shadowing deep to the triceps.
CRITICAL: The Radial Nerve appears as a hyperechoic oval structure at the deep border of the triceps, in the spiral groove of the humerus — it sits between the triceps and the bone.
At more proximal levels, all three heads (long, lateral, medial) can be distinguished by their fascial separations.
To confirm the long head: have the patient extend the elbow against resistance — the long head contracts prominently.
safetyNotes: The Radial Nerve runs in the spiral groove of the humerus, directly deep to the triceps — ALWAYS identify it before injecting.
Inject into the superficial-to-mid portion of the muscle belly — do not advance the needle to the bone.
The profunda brachii artery accompanies the radial nerve — use color Doppler to confirm.
The long head is safest to inject in the mid-substance away from the spiral groove.
ultrasound.videoSource: Dr. Andrei Bursuc — Long Head of Triceps Spasticity (Annotated US)

probePlacementHint: Patient seated or prone. Place probe transversely on posterior mid-upper arm. Photo from behind showing probe across triceps belly.
pearls: Rarely injected in spasticity — extended elbow is uncommon. Confirm the pattern
If injecting, protect elbow extension function as much as possible for reaching
Long head crosses the shoulder — may contribute to shoulder extension posturing
Extensor spasticity is less common than flexor; triceps injection is reserved for cases where the extension posture clearly contributes to function loss, positioning difficulty, or hygiene.
When treating extensors, always consider the action and loss-of-action of the opposing flexors and the shoulder muscles.
The three heads are not always clearly distinguishable clinically — US guidance helps target specific heads.
supplies: 25-27G needle (1.5 inch for superficial, 2-3 inch for deep)
dosageNote: Rarely injected for spasticity. Confirm genuine spasticity before treating.
dangerZones: The Radial Nerve runs in the spiral groove of the humerus, directly deep to the triceps — ALWAYS identify it before injecting.
Inject into the superficial-to-mid portion of the muscle belly — do not advance the needle to the bone.
The profunda brachii artery accompanies the radial nerve — use color Doppler to confirm.
The long head is safest to inject in the mid-substance away from the spiral groove.
positionLabel: Seated or prone · elbow flexed ~90°

name: Brachioradialis
landmarks: Lateral Epicondyle (palpate the bony prominence on the lateral distal humerus — it is the origin landmark for the mobile wad of muscles)
Radial Styloid (palpate the bony prominence at the distal lateral wrist — the brachioradialis inserts at the base of the styloid process)
Lateral Supracondylar Ridge (palpate the bony ridge running proximally from the lateral epicondyle along the lateral humerus — the muscle originates from its distal two-thirds)
Lateral supracondylar ridge of the humerus (origin) — palpate just above the lateral elbow.
Radial aspect of the forearm — the muscle forms the lateral border of the cubital fossa.
placement: Position the patient seated with the forearm resting on a table in neutral position (thumb pointing upward).
Identify the proximal third of the forearm on the lateral (radial) side.
Palpate the brachioradialis muscle belly — ask the patient to flex the elbow against resistance with the forearm in neutral to confirm its contraction.
The muscle belly is the most superficial and lateral muscle of the forearm, forming the lateral border of the cubital fossa.
Insert the needle into the bulk of the muscle belly at the junction of the proximal and middle thirds of the forearm, perpendicular to the skin.
Advance 1-1.5 cm — the muscle is superficial.
Stay lateral and superficial to avoid the radial nerve/posterior interosseous nerve, which courses deep to the brachioradialis.
Aspirate before injecting. A single injection into the mid-belly is usually sufficient.
Injection site: proximal third of the lateral forearm, into the muscle belly.
setup: Surface anatomy is usually sufficient — the muscle belly is easily palpable when the patient flexes the elbow with the forearm in neutral.
USG can confirm the needle is in brachioradialis and not in the deeper supinator or extensor muscles.
Mark the muscle belly with the forearm in neutral and the elbow flexed against resistance.

The radial nerve bifurcates into the superficial (sensory) branch and the posterior interosseous nerve (motor) deep to this muscle at the level of the radial head — stay proximal in the muscle belly and superficial.
Patient position: elbow flexed and in mid-position (neither fully supinated nor fully pronated).

ultrasound.probe: High-frequency linear (10-15 MHz), Samsung LA3-16AD recommended
ultrasound.orientation: Transverse (short-axis) over the lateral proximal forearm, approximately 4-6 cm distal to the lateral epicondyle
viewSteps: Place the probe transversely on the lateral forearm with the patient's elbow slightly flexed and forearm in neutral (thumb-up) position.
Identify the Brachioradialis as the most superficial muscle on the lateral side — it appears as a crescent-shaped hypoechoic structure directly under the subcutaneous tissue.
Deep and lateral to the Brachioradialis, identify the ECRL (Extensor Carpi Radialis Longus) — it sits adjacent to and partially beneath the BR.
Deep to both BR and ECRL, the large Brachialis muscle fills the deeper compartment wrapping around the lateral humerus.
CRITICAL LANDMARK: The Radial Nerve appears as a small hyperechoic oval structure in the fascial plane between the Brachioradialis and Brachialis — typically at the lateral-deep border of the BR.
To confirm identification: ask the patient to flex the elbow with the forearm in neutral — the BR will contract and thicken while the ECRL performs wrist extension.
safetyNotes: The Radial Nerve runs in the intermuscular septum between the Brachioradialis and Brachialis — always identify it before injecting.
Keep the needle tip superficial and within the BR muscle belly — do not advance past the fascial plane toward the radial nerve.
The radial recurrent artery may run near the radial nerve — use color Doppler if uncertain.
ultrasound.videoSource: Dr. Andrei Bursuc — Brachioradialis spasticity (Annotated US)

Under ultrasound, track the needle tip through the interosseous membrane and stop as soon as it enters the thin hypoechoic pronator quadratus muscle belly just superficial to the pronator line of the radius.
The muscle is thin (5-10 mm) — advance only the minimum distance needed to place the tip within it.
Aspirate before injecting. A single injection site is usually sufficient.
Injection site: deep to FCR/FDS in the distal anterior forearm.
Ventral approach (preferred): needle enters from the medial (ulnar) side of the distal anterior forearm, at a right angle to the forearm and slightly above the ulna.
Dorsal approach (alternative): possible but NOT preferred — the extensor tendons are in the way and the interosseous membrane must be penetrated. If used, the hand must be in supination.
Sites: typically 1.

Consider EMG guidance as an adjunct to confirm placement in this small deep muscle.
US guidance is strongly recommended — pronator quadratus lies deep to the superficial flexors and the median nerve/radial artery are in the vicinity.

US guidance strongly recommended — pronator quadratus cannot be palpated and lies deep to the superficial flexors.

To confirm muscle identification, ask the patient to pronate the forearm against resistance — pronator quadratus will contract.

name: Extensor Carpi Radialis Longus
landmarks: Lateral supracondylar ridge of the humerus (origin) — palpate just proximal to the lateral epicondyle.
Base of the second metacarpal (insertion) — dorsoradial hand.
Mobile wad of three (brachioradialis, ECRL, ECRB) — palpable on the radiodorsal proximal forearm with resisted wrist extension.
placement: Position the patient seated with the forearm pronated and resting on a flat surface to expose the dorsoradial forearm.
Identify the mobile wad on the radial-dorsal aspect of the proximal forearm, just distal to the elbow crease.
Ask the patient to extend the wrist with slight radial deviation against resistance — the ECRL belly stands out just dorsal to the brachioradialis.
Insert the needle into the muscle belly in the proximal third of the forearm, perpendicular to the skin.
Advance ~1-1.5 cm — the muscle is superficial within the mobile wad.
Aspirate before injecting; a single mid-belly injection is usually sufficient.
Stay superficial and radial — the posterior interosseous nerve lies deep, passing beneath the ECRB into the supinator.
setup: The mobile wad (brachioradialis, ECRL, ECRB) is easily palpable on the radiodorsal proximal forearm with resisted wrist extension.
Ultrasound helps separate ECRL from the brachioradialis (more volar) and ECRB (deeper).
Patient position: forearm pronated, wrist relaxed.

ultrasound.orientation: Transverse (short-axis) over the radiodorsal proximal forearm, ~3-5 cm distal to the lateral epicondyle
viewSteps: Place the probe transversely on the dorsoradial proximal forearm with the forearm pronated.
Identify the mobile wad: brachioradialis most superficial/volar, ECRL just dorsal to it, ECRB deep to the ECRL.
Ask for resisted wrist extension — the ECRL and ECRB thicken; the ECRL contracts with radial deviation.
Follow the muscles distally as they become tendinous in the mid-forearm.
safetyNotes: The posterior interosseous nerve (deep motor branch of the radial nerve) passes deep, between the ECRB and the supinator — keep the needle superficial in the ECRL belly.
The superficial (sensory) branch of the radial nerve runs beneath the brachioradialis on the radial side — avoid a too-volar approach.
The radial artery lies on the volar-radial forearm — stay dorsal.

probePlacementHint: Patient seated, forearm pronated on table. Place probe transversely on the radiodorsal proximal forearm, 3-5 cm below the lateral epicondyle, over the mobile wad.
pearls: ECRL and ECRB are the prime wrist extensors — usually the lengthened antagonists in wrist-flexion spasticity, so they are targets mainly in extension dystonia or mixed patterns.
ECRL is innervated by the radial nerve proper (proximal to the PIN); ECRB usually by the deep branch/PIN.
Inject with the forearm pronated to bring the mobile wad uppermost.
dosageNote: Draft entry — extensor data added for completeness (dystonia / mixed patterns). Verify every dose, US note, and hazard against current labeling and a primary source before clinical use.
dangerZones: The posterior interosseous nerve passes deep, between the ECRB and the supinator — keep the needle superficial in the ECRL belly and do not advance toward the radial neck.
The superficial radial (sensory) nerve runs beneath the brachioradialis — avoid a too-volar/radial approach.
The radial artery lies on the volar-radial forearm — stay dorsal.
positionLabel: Seated · forearm pronated on a flat surface

name: Extensor Carpi Radialis Brevis
landmarks: Lateral epicondyle of the humerus via the common extensor origin.
Base of the third metacarpal (insertion).
Mobile wad — ECRB lies deep to the ECRL on the radiodorsal proximal forearm.
placement: Position the patient seated with the forearm pronated and resting on a flat surface.
Identify the mobile wad on the radiodorsal proximal forearm; the ECRB lies deep to the ECRL.
Ask the patient to extend the wrist in neutral against resistance — the ECRB is the main wrist extensor and thickens deep to the ECRL.
Insert the needle into the proximal third of the forearm, angling slightly deeper than the ECRL.
Advance ~1.5-2 cm to reach the deeper ECRB belly.
Aspirate before injecting; confirm depth with ultrasound when possible.
Do NOT advance toward the radial neck — the posterior interosseous nerve enters the supinator immediately deep here.
setup: ECRB sits deep to ECRL — ultrasound is recommended to confirm the correct (deeper) belly.
ECRB is the principal wrist extensor and the usual antagonist in spastic wrist flexion.
Patient position: forearm pronated, wrist relaxed.

ultrasound.orientation: Transverse over the radiodorsal proximal forearm, ~4-6 cm distal to the lateral epicondyle
viewSteps: Place the probe transversely on the dorsoradial proximal forearm, forearm pronated.
Identify ECRL superficially and ECRB immediately deep to it, overlying the radius.
Deep to ECRB, identify the supinator wrapping the radial neck — the posterior interosseous nerve runs within it.
Resisted wrist extension in neutral thickens the ECRB to confirm identity.
safetyNotes: The posterior interosseous nerve runs in the supinator immediately deep to the ECRB at the radial neck — keep the needle in the superficial-to-mid ECRB belly and never advance to the radial neck.
Use ultrasound to confirm you are in ECRB and not in the supinator/PIN plane.
Stay dorsal to the radial artery.

probePlacementHint: Patient seated, forearm pronated. Place probe transversely on the radiodorsal proximal forearm, 4-6 cm below the lateral epicondyle; ECRB lies deep to ECRL over the radius.
pearls: ECRB is the principal wrist extensor — the key antagonist that is usually lengthened in spastic wrist flexion.
It lies deep to ECRL; ultrasound confirms the correct belly.
Highest posterior-interosseous-nerve risk of the wrist extensors because the PIN enters the supinator just deep and proximal.
dosageNote: Draft entry — extensor data added for completeness (dystonia / mixed patterns). Verify every dose, US note, and hazard against current labeling and a primary source before clinical use.
dangerZones: The posterior interosseous nerve enters the supinator immediately deep and proximal to the ECRB at the radial neck — keep the needle superficial-to-mid in the belly and never advance toward the radial neck.
ECRB sits deep to ECRL — confirm the plane with ultrasound to avoid the deeper supinator/PIN.
Stay dorsal to the radial artery on the volar-radial forearm.
positionLabel: Seated · forearm pronated on a flat surface

name: Adductor Pollicis
landmarks: First Web Space (palpate the fleshy area between the thumb and index finger metacarpals on the dorsal hand — the adductor pollicis fills this web space; squeeze the web space between your thumb and index finger to feel the muscle bulk)

Third Metacarpal (palpate the long bone of the middle finger on the dorsal hand — the oblique head of the adductor pollicis originates from the base of the second and third metacarpals and the capitate)
Proximal Phalanx of the Thumb, Ulnar Side (palpate the base of the thumb proximal phalanx on the ulnar side — the adductor pollicis inserts here via the ulnar sesamoid bone)
First web space of the hand — adductor pollicis forms the deep floor.
Transverse head (along the 3rd metacarpal) and oblique head — the muscle is two-headed.
placement: Position the patient with the hand resting on a flat surface, palm down (pronated), with the thumb abducted away from the palm.
Identify the first web space between the thumb and index finger metacarpals.
Palpate the adductor pollicis — ask the patient to adduct the thumb firmly against the index finger; feel the muscle contract and bulk in the web space.
The muscle has two heads: the oblique head (deeper, originating from the carpals and metacarpals) and the transverse head (more superficial, originating from the third metacarpal shaft).
Insert the needle from the dorsal aspect of the first web space, perpendicular to the plane of the hand.
Advance 0.5-1 cm — this is a thin muscle in a confined space.
Stay within the web space and do not advance toward the palmar surface where the digital neurovascular bundles run.
Aspirate before injecting. A single injection into the bulk of the web space is usually sufficient. Use a small-gauge needle (25-27G).
Injection site: into the first web space, toward the 3rd metacarpal.
Sites: 1-2.
setup: USG is helpful but the muscle can be injected reliably using surface anatomy in the first web space.
Use a dorsal approach to avoid the palmar digital nerves and arteries.
Have the patient adduct the thumb to confirm the muscle belly before marking.
Differentiate from the first dorsal interosseous, which lies dorsal and lateral in the web space — the adductor pollicis is deeper and more palmar.
End branches of the radial artery run nearby — identify on US with Doppler.

ultrasound.probe: High-frequency linear (10-15 MHz); a hockey-stick probe is helpful in the tight first web space
ultrasound.orientation: Transverse across the first web space from the dorsal approach
viewSteps: Identify the subcutaneous fat and thin dorsal skin as the most superficial layers.
The first dorsal interosseous appears as a superficial hypoechoic muscle on the dorsal-radial aspect of the web space.
Deep to the first dorsal interosseous, the adductor pollicis appears as a hypoechoic muscle filling the space between the first and second metacarpals on the palmar side.
The first and second metacarpals appear as two bright hyperechoic cortical lines on either side of the web space.
The deep palmar arch and digital arteries may be seen with color Doppler on the palmar surface of the adductor pollicis.
safetyNotes: The deep branch of the ulnar nerve passes through the adductor pollicis (between the two heads) — use a superficial injection into the transverse head when possible.
The radialis indicis artery and princeps pollicis artery run along the borders of the web space — stay in the central bulk of the muscle.
The palmar digital nerves run on the palmar aspect — use a dorsal approach and do not advance through the full depth of the web space.

probePlacementHint: Patient hand pronated on table. Place small linear or hockey-stick probe transversely across first web space from dorsal approach. Photo from above showing probe on dorsal thumb web space.
pearls: Key target for thumb-in-palm deformity (thumb adduction component)
Very small — use hockey-stick probe and minimal doses (10-20U Botox)
Key for thumb-in-palm deformity along with FPL and FPB.
dosageNote: Very small muscle — low doses only. Dorsal approach preferred.
dangerZones: Dorsal approach is safer — avoids thenar neurovascular structures
Two-headed muscle (transverse and oblique heads) — injection errors are common if you inject too superficially (hits dorsal interosseous instead).
positionLabel: Hand resting palm-down, thumb abducted

name: Hand Lumbricals
landmarks: Metacarpal Heads (palpate the knuckles — the lumbricals lie on the radial side of each FDP tendon in the palm, just proximal to the MCP joints)
Palmar Crease (the distal palmar crease runs across the MCP joints — the lumbricals sit just proximal to this crease in the deep palm)
Metacarpal bones — use them as the palpation reference.
Radial aspect of each respective tendon at the upper half of the metacarpal.
Upper half of the palm, radial to each respective flexor tendon (lumbricals 1-4 each sit radial to the flexor digitorum profundus tendon of their respective finger).
For the 1st lumbrical: directly above the distal border of the 2nd metacarpal.
For the 2nd-4th lumbricals: slightly distal and radial to the head of the respective metacarpal (3rd, 4th, 5th).
placement: Position the patient with the hand supinated (palm up), fingers relaxed and slightly extended.
The lumbricals are four small muscles in the palm, each on the radial (thumb) side of the corresponding FDP tendon to fingers 2-5.
Target the 1st and 2nd lumbricals first (radial side) — they are the most commonly spastic and most accessible.
PALMAR APPROACH: Insert the needle into the palm just proximal to the MCP joint of the target finger, on the radial side of the flexor tendon.
Advance only 5-10 mm — the lumbricals are very small and superficial in the palmar space.
USG or EMG guidance is strongly recommended given the small size and proximity to digital neurovascular bundles.
Aspirate before injecting. Use very small volumes (0.1-0.2 mL per lumbrical) to avoid diffusion.
Inject only the clinically affected lumbricals — do not blanket all four unless all are spastic.
Injection site: radial to each respective flexor tendon, approximately in the upper half of the metacarpal.
Primary approach (palmar): needle enters from the palmar side, radial to each respective tendon at the specified landmarks.
Alternative approach (dorsal): possible from the dorsum of the hand. Place the US probe in the palm and inject from the dorsum so the needle enters the image from below the screen.
Injection direction: toward the bones (metacarpals).
Sites: 1 per lumbrical, as many lumbricals as clinically indicated.
setup: USG with a high-frequency linear or hockey-stick probe is recommended — the lumbricals are very small and surrounded by tendons and neurovascular structures.
EMG guidance is an excellent adjunct — confirm the muscle is electrically active during MCP flexion with IP extension.
The proper digital nerves and arteries run immediately adjacent to each lumbrical — identify them on US or use extreme caution with landmark technique.
Very low doses and volumes are essential — diffusion to adjacent FDP/FDS tendons or interossei can cause unintended weakness.
Patient position: elbow in supination with the hand resting palm-up.
Patient position: elbow in supination, wrist and fingers comfortably extended.
US guidance strongly recommended — the lumbricals cannot be palpated, and injection errors or diffusion into adjacent muscles occur easily.

ultrasound.probe: High-frequency linear (10-15 MHz); hockey-stick probe preferred for the tight palmar space
ultrasound.orientation: Longitudinal along the metacarpal shaft on the palmar surface, or transverse across the palm at the MCP level
viewSteps: Place the probe longitudinally on the palmar surface along the metacarpal of the target finger.
Identify the FDP and FDS tendons as hyperechoic linear structures running along the metacarpal.
The lumbrical appears as a small hypoechoic muscle belly on the radial side of the FDP tendon, just proximal to the MCP joint.
In transverse view, the lumbrical is a small oval hypoechoic structure between the FDP tendons of adjacent fingers.
The proper digital nerve and artery run immediately adjacent — they appear as a small hyperechoic dot (nerve) and anechoic circle (artery).
To confirm: ask the patient to flex the MCP while extending the IP joints — the lumbrical will contract.
safetyNotes: The proper digital nerves and arteries run immediately adjacent to the lumbricals — always identify them before injecting.
The flexor tendons (FDP/FDS) are immediately deep — do not advance past the lumbrical into the tendon sheath.
Use the smallest possible volume to prevent diffusion to adjacent structures.
The 1st and 2nd lumbricals are innervated by the median nerve; the 3rd and 4th by the ulnar nerve — toxin spread could weaken intrinsic hand function.

dosageNote: Per individual lumbrical. Very small muscles — start at the low end. Total hand lumbrical dose typically 10-25 U Botox across affected digits.
probePlacementHint: Patient palm-up, fingers relaxed. Place hockey-stick probe longitudinally on palm along the metacarpal. Photo from palmar view showing probe on mid-palm.
pearls: The 'hidden' cause of intrinsic-plus hand — if MCP flexion persists despite treating FDS/FDP, the lumbricals may be the culprit
1st and 2nd lumbricals (median nerve) are more commonly spastic than 3rd and 4th (ulnar nerve)
Tiny muscles requiring tiny doses — 5-10 U Botox per lumbrical is usually sufficient; overdosing weakens grip
EMG confirmation is especially valuable here since the muscles are so small and surrounded by tendons
Many physiatrists suspect only a minor effect and refrain from injecting the lumbricals — consider with caution and reserve for clear intrinsic-plus deformity.
The lumbricals cannot be palpated; injection errors and toxin diffusion into adjacent muscles occur easily without US.
The 1st lumbrical must be distinguished from adductor pollicis and the 1st dorsal interosseous — US shows this clearly.
Lumbrical spasticity contributes to the 'lumbrical hand' deformity (MCP flexion + IP extension). Reserve treatment for this clear pattern.
Effect of lumbrical injection is debated — many clinicians report only modest benefit. Set patient expectations accordingly.

dangerZones: The proper digital nerves and arteries run immediately adjacent to the lumbricals — always identify them before injecting.
The flexor tendons (FDP/FDS) are immediately deep — do not advance past the lumbrical into the tendon sheath.

name: Iliopsoas
landmarks: Anterior Superior Iliac Spine (ASIS) (palpate the bony projection at the anterior end of the iliac crest — the iliopsoas passes just medial to this landmark as it descends toward the hip)
Inguinal Ligament (palpate the firm band running from the ASIS to the pubic tubercle — the iliopsoas passes deep to this structure as it exits the pelvis)

Lesser Trochanter (not directly palpable, but located on the posteromedial aspect of the proximal femur approximately 5 cm below the inguinal ligament — this is the insertion point of the iliopsoas tendon)
placement: Position the patient supine with the hip in neutral position and the knee extended.
Identify the femoral artery pulse just below the inguinal ligament — the iliopsoas lies immediately lateral to the femoral neurovascular bundle.
The injection site is approximately 2-3 cm distal to the inguinal ligament, lateral to the femoral artery pulsation.
USG guidance is mandatory for this injection due to the proximity of the femoral neurovascular bundle.
Under ultrasound guidance, insert the needle lateral to the femoral vessels and advance toward the iliopsoas muscle belly.
Advance approximately 2-4 cm to reach the muscle belly deep to the sartorius and rectus femoris. Aspirate before injecting. Distribute the dose across 1-2 sites.
setup: USG guidance is mandatory — blind injection of the iliopsoas carries significant risk of femoral nerve or vascular injury.
Have the patient flex the hip against resistance to confirm the correct muscle on ultrasound (the iliopsoas will be seen contracting).

The femoral nerve sits in the fascial groove BETWEEN the iliacus and psoas major (not medial to iliopsoas) — it lies on the anterior surface of the iliacus, deep to the iliopsoas fascia, and lateral to the femoral artery. It must be identified and avoided.
The femoral artery and vein lie medial to the iliopsoas — always confirm their location with color Doppler before inserting the needle.

ultrasound.probe: Low-frequency curvilinear (5-8 MHz) or high-frequency linear (10-15 MHz) in thin patients
ultrasound.orientation: Transverse across the proximal anterior thigh, 2-3 cm distal to the inguinal ligament, lateral to the femoral vessels
viewSteps: Identify subcutaneous fat, the fascia lata, and the Sartorius muscle as the most superficial structures laterally.
Medially, identify the Femoral Artery (pulsating) and Femoral Vein (compressible) within the femoral triangle.

Lateral to the femoral vessels, identify the Femoral Nerve as a hyperechoic triangular/oval structure sitting in the groove BETWEEN psoas major (medial) and iliacus (lateral), on the anterior iliacus surface.
Deep to the Sartorius and lateral to the femoral vessels, the Iliopsoas appears as a large oval hypoechoic muscle with a central hyperechoic tendon.
The Iliacus component lies laterally and the Psoas Major lies medially — the femoral nerve runs in the cleft between them. Direct the needle into the muscle belly AWAY from this groove.
Deep to the iliopsoas, identify the anterior acetabular rim or femoral head as a hyperechoic curved line.
safetyNotes: The femoral artery and vein lie medial to the iliopsoas — always use color Doppler to map the vessels before needle insertion.

CRITICAL: The femoral nerve runs WITHIN the iliopsoas complex, in the groove between iliacus (lateral) and psoas major (medial). It is NOT simply medial to iliopsoas. Identify it as a hyperechoic honeycomb structure and direct the needle to the muscle belly away from this cleft.
The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve runs near the ASIS and may cross the field — note its position if visible.
Do not inject too medially — this risks entering the femoral triangle and injuring the neurovascular bundle.

probePlacementHint: Patient supine, hip neutral. Place curvilinear probe transversely on proximal anterior thigh, 2-3 cm below inguinal ligament, lateral to femoral vessels. Photo from front showing probe in inguinal/proximal thigh region.
pearls: Primary hip flexor — the most important muscle for hip flexion spasticity
Deep target requiring curvilinear probe and careful technique
supplies: Ultrasound machine with curvilinear probe (5-8 MHz, for deep muscles)
22-25G spinal needle (3.5 inch for deep muscles)
dangerZones: Femoral nerve, artery, and vein are right next door — always identify with color Doppler
positionLabel: Supine · hip neutral, knee extended

name: Piriformis
landmarks: PSIS (Posterior Superior Iliac Spine — palpate the bony dimple on each side of the low back, at the level of S2)
Greater Trochanter (palpate the bony prominence on the lateral hip — the piriformis inserts on its superior-medial surface)
Sacral Hiatus (palpate the small bony depression at the distal sacrum/proximal coccyx in the midline — the piriformis originates from the anterior sacrum)
Greater trochanter of the femur (insertion).
Sacrum (origin) — piriformis runs from the anterior sacrum through the greater sciatic foramen.
Depth anchor: approximately 6-12 cm from skin depending on body habitus.
placement: Position the patient prone with a pillow under the pelvis to slightly flex the hips.
Palpate the PSIS and the Greater Trochanter — draw a line connecting these two landmarks.
Identify the midpoint of this PSIS-to-Greater-Trochanter line — this is your injection site.
The piriformis lies deep to the Gluteus Maximus at this location.
Insert the needle perpendicular to the skin surface at the midpoint.
Advance through the Gluteus Maximus (typically 4-6 cm depending on body habitus) until the needle tip enters the piriformis.
You may feel a subtle change in tissue resistance as you pass through the fascial plane between the two muscles.
Aspirate before injecting. Inject slowly and monitor for any sciatic symptoms (radiating pain down the leg).
Injection site: along a line from the greater trochanter to the sacrum, approximately halfway.
setup: USG guidance is ESSENTIAL — the sciatic nerve exits the pelvis immediately inferior to the piriformis belly.
EMG guidance may be used as an adjunct to confirm needle placement within the piriformis.
If the patient reports radiating pain down the leg during needle advancement, STOP and reposition — you may be near the sciatic nerve.
The piriformis is a relatively small, deep muscle — precise needle placement is critical.
CT or fluoroscopic guidance is strongly recommended if at all possible — piriformis lies adjacent to the sciatic nerve.
If CT/fluoroscopy unavailable, US with Doppler to identify inferior gluteal vessels, plus EMG confirmation.
Patient position: prone with hip internally rotated to expose the muscle.

ultrasound.orientation: Transverse along the line from PSIS to Greater Trochanter, centered at the midpoint
viewSteps: Identify the subcutaneous tissue and the thick Gluteus Maximus as a large superficial hypoechoic muscle.
Deep to the Gluteus Maximus, identify the hyperechoic fascial plane — the piriformis lies just below this.
The Piriformis appears as a smaller, flat hypoechoic muscle running obliquely from the sacrum toward the greater trochanter.
Deep to the piriformis, the hyperechoic bony landmarks of the posterior ilium/sacrum provide a deep boundary.
The sciatic nerve appears as a large hyperechoic oval structure (honeycomb pattern on cross-section) immediately inferior to the piriformis.
safetyNotes: The sciatic nerve exits immediately inferior to the piriformis — always identify it on ultrasound before injecting.
The inferior gluteal artery runs near the inferior border of the piriformis — use color Doppler to locate it.
The pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels exit medial to the piriformis — avoid directing the needle medially.
