probePlacementHint: Patient prone, pillow under pelvis. Place curvilinear probe transversely along PSIS-to-greater-trochanter line, at midpoint. Photo showing probe between PSIS and GT.
pearls: Notoriously difficult to isolate on US — confirm with EMG if available
Often co-injected with other hip external rotators for combined pattern
Sciatic-nerve proximity is the dominant safety concern — never inject without image guidance.
supplies: Ultrasound machine with curvilinear probe (5-8 MHz, for deep muscles)
22-25G spinal needle (3.5 inch for deep muscles)
dangerZones: Sciatic nerve runs immediately inferior to (or through) this muscle — USG is essential, and EMG can be a useful adjunct to confirm you are in piriformis rather than adjacent muscles.
positionLabel: Prone · pillow under the pelvis

name: Pectineus
landmarks: Superior pubic ramus / pectineal line (origin) — palpable in the groin medial to the femoral pulse.
Femoral triangle — the pectineus forms part of its floor, immediately medial to the femoral vein.
Pectineal line of the femur, just below the lesser trochanter (insertion), high in the medial thigh.
placement: Position the patient supine with the hip slightly abducted and externally rotated (frog-leg) to open the groin and femoral triangle.
Palpate the femoral pulse — the femoral artery and vein mark the LATERAL edge of the pectineus.
Under ultrasound, identify the pectineus as the flat muscle on the superior pubic ramus, medial to the femoral vein and deep/lateral to the adductor longus.
Insert the needle from MEDIAL to lateral into the pectineus belly, keeping the femoral vessels in view at all times.
Advance ~1.5-3 cm to the muscle on the pubic ramus.
Aspirate before injecting — the femoral vein lies immediately lateral.
Use ultrasound for every injection; never advance the needle toward the vessels.
setup: Ultrasound is STRONGLY recommended — the pectineus sits immediately medial to the femoral vein in the femoral triangle.
Palpate and mark the femoral pulse first; approach the muscle from the medial side.
Patient position: supine, hip abducted and externally rotated to expose the groin.

ultrasound.orientation: Transverse across the femoral triangle, just distal to the inguinal ligament
viewSteps: Place the probe transversely in the groin just below the inguinal crease and identify the femoral artery and vein with color Doppler.
Medial to the femoral vein, identify the pectineus as a flat muscle overlying the superior pubic ramus.
The adductor longus lies medial and superficial; the pectineus is deeper, against the bone.
Keep the femoral vessels in view and approach the pectineus from the medial side.
safetyNotes: The femoral vein, artery, and nerve lie immediately lateral in the femoral triangle — identify them with color Doppler and approach from MEDIAL to lateral; aspirate before injecting.
The anterior branch of the obturator nerve runs deep between the pectineus and the adductor brevis / obturator externus.
Never advance the needle toward the femoral vessels — this is an ultrasound-only target.

probePlacementHint: Patient supine, hip abducted/externally rotated. Place probe transversely in the groin just below the inguinal crease; identify the femoral vessels (Doppler) and the pectineus just medial to the femoral vein.
pearls: Hip flexor AND adductor in the femoral triangle — a useful add-on for scissoring/adduction with a hip-flexion component.
Sits immediately medial to the femoral vein — an ultrasound-only target for most injectors.
Approach medial-to-lateral to keep the needle path away from the femoral vessels.
dosageNote: Draft entry — added for completeness; doses are illustrative starting references. Verify every dose, ultrasound note, and hazard against current labeling and a primary source before clinical use.
dangerZones: The femoral vein, artery, and nerve lie immediately lateral in the femoral triangle — identify them with color Doppler, approach from medial to lateral, and aspirate before injecting.
The anterior branch of the obturator nerve runs deep between the pectineus and the adductor brevis / obturator externus.
Ultrasound-only target — never advance the needle toward the femoral vessels.
positionLabel: Supine · frog-leg (hip abducted & externally rotated)

name: Adductor Longus
landmarks: Pubic Tubercle (palpate the bony prominence on the superior pubic ramus just lateral to the pubic symphysis — the adductor longus tendon originates here as a prominent, palpable cord)
Medial Femoral Condyle (palpate the large bony prominence on the inner aspect of the distal femur — the adductor longus inserts along the middle third of the linea aspera proximal to this)

Adductor Longus Tendon (with the hip slightly abducted and flexed, palpate the most prominent tendon in the proximal medial thigh originating from the pubic tubercle — this is the superficial border of the muscle)
Pubic tubercle — palpate the adductor longus tendon at its origin.
Medial condyle of the tibia — adductor longus inserts along the middle third of the linea aspera.
Anchor: 4 fingers (approximately 7-8 cm) distal to the pubic tubercle, along the adductor group.
placement: Position the patient supine with the hip slightly abducted and externally rotated, and the knee flexed with the sole of the foot resting against the opposite knee (frog-leg position).
Identify the adductor longus tendon — it is the most prominent and superficial tendon in the proximal medial thigh, easily palpable as a taut cord originating from the pubic tubercle.
The injection site is approximately 3-5 cm distal to the pubic tubercle along the muscle belly, in the medial thigh.
Insert the needle perpendicular to the skin into the muscle belly just lateral to the palpable tendon.
Advance approximately 1.5-2.5 cm — the adductor longus is the most superficial muscle in the medial compartment at this level.
Aspirate before injecting. Distribute the dose across 2 sites along the proximal muscle belly.
Injection site: palpate the adductor longus tendon at the pubic tubercle, then move approximately 4 fingers (7-8 cm) distal, into the muscle belly.
setup: USG is strongly recommended to avoid the femoral neurovascular bundle, which lies lateral to the adductor longus in the femoral triangle.
Have the patient adduct the hip against resistance to confirm the correct muscle belly before injection.
The profunda femoris artery runs deep to the adductor longus — do not advance the needle too deeply.
The obturator nerve anterior branch runs on the superficial surface of the adductor brevis, deep to the adductor longus — ultrasound helps avoid it.
Patient position: supine, hip slightly flexed and abducted.

ultrasound.orientation: Transverse across the proximal medial thigh, 3-5 cm distal to the pubic tubercle
viewSteps: Identify subcutaneous fat and the fascia lata as the superficial layers.
The Adductor Longus appears as a triangular or oval hypoechoic muscle belly immediately deep to the fascia — it is the most superficial adductor at this level.
Deep to the Adductor Longus, identify a bright hyperechoic fascial plane separating it from the Adductor Brevis.
The Adductor Brevis appears as a second hypoechoic muscle layer deep to the longus.
Deep to the Adductor Brevis, identify the Adductor Magnus as the largest and deepest muscle in this compartment.
Laterally, identify the femoral vessels (artery pulsating, vein compressible) — ensure the injection stays medial to these structures.
safetyNotes: The femoral artery and vein lie lateral to the adductor longus in the femoral triangle — always confirm their location with color Doppler before injecting.
The profunda femoris artery courses deep to the adductor longus — avoid deep needle advancement beyond the muscle belly.
The anterior branch of the obturator nerve runs between the adductor longus and adductor brevis — stay within the substance of the adductor longus.

probePlacementHint: Patient supine, hip slightly abducted and externally rotated. Place probe transversely on proximal medial thigh, 3-5 cm below pubic tubercle. Photo showing probe on inner proximal thigh.
pearls: Most superficial adductor — the 'go-to' for adductor spasticity injection
Palpable as the prominent tendon in the proximal medial thigh with hip abduction
Femoral vessels lie LATERAL to the adductor longus in the femoral triangle — identify them with color Doppler and keep the needle medial to these structures.
The adductors cannot be differentiated from one another with certainty by palpation — US guidance is recommended if targeting specifically.
supplies: 25-27G needle (1.5 inch for superficial, 2-3 inch for deep)
dangerZones: Going too deep risks hitting adductor magnus; too far lateral or posterior risks gracilis.
positionLabel: Supine · frog-leg (hip abducted & externally rotated)

name: Adductor Brevis
landmarks: Pubic Tubercle (palpate the bony prominence on the superior pubic ramus medially — the adductor brevis originates from the body and inferior ramus of the pubis, just lateral to gracilis)
Adductor Longus Tendon (palpate the prominent cord in the proximal medial thigh with the hip slightly abducted — the adductor brevis lies immediately deep to adductor longus)
Pubic tubercle — palpate the adductor longus tendon at its origin (brevis lies deep and behind it).
Anchor: 4 fingers (approximately 7-8 cm) distal from the pubic tubercle, 3-5 cm deep through the overlying adductor longus.
placement: Position the patient supine with the hip abducted 30-45 degrees, knee flexed, and the leg externally rotated (frog-leg position).
Identify the adductor longus tendon at its pubic origin — palpate the firm cord at the medial groin crease.
The adductor brevis lies DEEP to the adductor longus. It cannot be reliably distinguished by palpation alone.
USG is strongly recommended — insert the needle through the adductor longus to reach the adductor brevis layer deep to it.
Under ultrasound, advance the needle through the adductor longus until the tip crosses the fascial plane into the deeper adductor brevis muscle belly.
Confirm depth — adductor brevis lies between adductor longus (superficial) and adductor magnus/obturator externus (deep).
Aspirate before injecting. A single injection into the mid-belly is usually sufficient.
Avoid advancing too deeply past adductor brevis into the obturator externus or adductor magnus unless those are also targets.
Injection site: palpate the tendon at the pubic tubercle origin; inject 4 fingers (7-8 cm) distal and 3-5 cm deep through the skin.
Sites: 1-2, usually one site.
Injection depth: 3-5 cm depending on muscle thickness.
setup: USG guidance is strongly recommended — adductor brevis is deep to adductor longus and cannot be reliably injected by landmark alone.
The obturator nerve (anterior branch) runs on the superficial surface of adductor brevis between it and adductor longus — identify it and avoid direct injection into the nerve.
The posterior branch of the obturator nerve runs between adductor brevis and adductor magnus — it may be visible deep to the target on US.
The profunda femoris artery and its branches run in this plane — use color Doppler to identify vessels before needle insertion.
Patient position: supine, hip slightly flexed and abducted, knee slightly flexed.
US guidance recommended — adductor brevis lies between longus (anterior) and magnus (posterior); hard to target blindly.

ultrasound.orientation: Transverse across the proximal medial thigh, at the level of the adductor longus origin, perpendicular to the muscle fibers
viewSteps: Place the probe transversely on the proximal medial thigh with the hip abducted.
Identify the adductor longus as the most superficial adductor — a large hypoechoic muscle belly with a prominent proximal tendon originating from the pubic tubercle.
Deep to adductor longus, identify a thin fascial plane — the adductor brevis lies immediately deep to this fascia as a smaller hypoechoic muscle.
The anterior branch of the obturator nerve may be visible as a small hyperechoic structure in the fascial plane between adductor longus and brevis.
Deep to adductor brevis, the adductor magnus fills the deepest compartment.
Use color Doppler to identify the profunda femoris artery and its perforating branches, which run in the inter-muscular planes.
safetyNotes: The anterior branch of the obturator nerve runs between adductor longus and brevis — identify it and keep the needle tip within the muscle belly, not in the inter-fascial plane.
The profunda femoris artery and perforating branches course through the adductor compartment — use Doppler before each needle insertion.
Do not advance past adductor brevis into the deeper compartment unless targeting adductor magnus.

dosageNote: Often co-injected with adductor longus and magnus for refractory scissoring.
probePlacementHint: Patient supine, frog-leg position. Place probe transversely on proximal medial thigh at the adductor longus origin. Photo from medial view showing probe on inner thigh.
pearls: The 'hidden' adductor — lies deep to adductor longus and is often missed when only the superficial adductor longus is injected
If scissoring persists after treating adductor longus alone, add adductor brevis (and magnus) to the injection set
Anterior branch of obturator nerve sits right on top of this muscle — always identify it on US before injecting
supplies: 25-27G needle (1.5 inch for superficial, 2-3 inch for deep)
dangerZones: Going too far lateral hits adductor longus (not the target).
Going too far medial or too deep hits adductor magnus.
Going too far dorsomedial (posteromedial) penetrates gracilis instead.
positionLabel: Supine · frog-leg (hip abducted & externally rotated)

name: Adductor Magnus
landmarks: Ischial Tuberosity (palpate the large bony prominence at the inferior aspect of the pelvis in the buttock crease — the hamstring portion of the adductor magnus originates here)
Inferior Pubic Ramus (palpate the bony ridge extending inferolaterally from the pubic symphysis — the adductor portion of the muscle originates along this ridge)

Adductor Tubercle (palpate the small bony prominence on the medial supracondylar ridge of the distal femur just above the medial epicondyle — the hamstring portion of the adductor magnus inserts here)
Pubic tubercle and ischial tuberosity (combined origin).
Linea aspera of the femur (insertion).
Anchor: 10-13 cm distal to the pubic tubercle for proximal injection; additional sites at 4 fingers (7-8 cm) intervals along the adductor line.
placement: Position the patient prone with the legs slightly apart, or supine with the hip abducted and externally rotated.
Identify the adductor magnus — it is the deepest and largest muscle of the medial thigh compartment, best accessed from the posterior-medial approach.
The injection site is at the junction of the middle and distal thirds of the medial thigh, posterior to the gracilis and adductor longus.
Insert the needle from the posteromedial aspect of the thigh, angling slightly anteriorly.
Advance approximately 2.5-4 cm — the adductor magnus is a deep muscle and the needle must traverse the more superficial adductors or approach from the posterior aspect.
Aspirate before injecting. Distribute the dose across 2-3 sites within the muscle belly due to its large size.
Injection site: multiple sites along the medial thigh, on a line from origin toward the linea aspera.
Sites: 1-3.
When injecting at two sites, position them on the same line rather than perpendicular — adductor magnus is long and oriented vertically.
setup: USG guidance is strongly recommended due to the depth of this muscle and the proximity of the sciatic nerve and profunda femoris vessels.
Have the patient adduct the hip forcefully against resistance to help identify the muscle bulk.
The sciatic nerve runs lateral and posterior to the adductor magnus in the posterior thigh — confirm its location with ultrasound.
The adductor hiatus (gap in the distal adductor magnus) transmits the femoral vessels into the popliteal fossa — avoid injecting near the distal muscle.
Patient position: supine, leg slightly flexed and abducted.

ultrasound.probe: Low-frequency curvilinear (5-8 MHz) or high-frequency linear (10-15 MHz) for thinner patients
ultrasound.orientation: Transverse across the posteromedial thigh at the junction of the middle and distal thirds
viewSteps: Identify subcutaneous fat and the deep fascia as the superficial layers.
The Gracilis and Adductor Longus appear as superficial hypoechoic muscles in the medial compartment.
Deep to these, identify the Adductor Brevis as an intermediate hypoechoic muscle layer.
The Adductor Magnus appears as the largest and deepest hypoechoic muscle mass, lying against the posterior surface of the femur.
Identify the femur as a hyperechoic curved line with acoustic shadowing deep to the adductor magnus.
Locate the profunda femoris vessels between the adductor muscles using color Doppler — they course between the adductor longus and adductor magnus.
safetyNotes: The profunda femoris artery and vein run between the adductor longus and adductor magnus — use color Doppler to identify and avoid these vessels.
The sciatic nerve lies posterolateral to the adductor magnus in the posterior compartment — do not direct the needle too far laterally or posteriorly.
The femoral artery transitions to the popliteal artery through the adductor hiatus distally — avoid injecting in the distal third of the muscle.
The posterior branch of the obturator nerve runs on the anterior surface of the adductor magnus — ultrasound helps minimize nerve injury.

probePlacementHint: Patient prone, legs slightly apart. Place probe transversely on posteromedial thigh at junction of middle and distal thirds. Photo from behind showing probe on posteromedial distal thigh.
pearls: Largest adductor — requires higher doses and multiple injection sites
Deep position makes US guidance essential
Adducts the free-swinging thigh; when standing, its most important action is stabilizing the femur together with TFL.
A very strong muscle — dose tends to be at the higher end of the adductor-group range.
supplies: Ultrasound machine with curvilinear probe (5-8 MHz, for deep muscles)
22-25G spinal needle (3.5 inch for deep muscles)
dangerZones: Sciatic nerve runs posterior — inject from medial approach to stay safe
positionLabel: Prone, legs apart (or supine, hip abducted & ER)

name: Gracilis
pattern: Hip adduction + knee flexion (crosses both joints)
landmarks: Pubic Symphysis (palpate the midline bony prominence — gracilis originates from the inferior pubic ramus near the symphysis, the most medial of the adductor origins)
Pes Anserinus (palpate the medial tibial flare below the knee — gracilis inserts here along with semitendinosus and sartorius; it is the middle tendon of the three)
Pubic tubercle (origin).
Medial condyle of the tibia (insertion).
Anchor: middle of a line between the pubic tubercle and the medial tibial condyle.
placement: Position the patient supine with the hip abducted 30-45 degrees and knee slightly flexed.
Identify the gracilis as the most superficial and medial muscle of the adductor group — it forms a thin strap running the full length of the medial thigh.
Palpate the thin muscle belly on the medial thigh — ask the patient to adduct the hip against resistance while you feel for contraction medially.
The injection site is the proximal third of the medial thigh, where the muscle belly is thickest.
Insert the needle perpendicular to the skin on the medial thigh into the superficial muscle belly.
Advance only 1-1.5 cm — gracilis is thin and superficial.
Aspirate before injecting. A single injection into the proximal belly is usually sufficient.
Stay superficial — the adductor longus and brevis lie deep to gracilis.
Injection site: middle of the line between the pubic tubercle and the medial tibial condyle, into the long thin muscle belly.
Sites: 1-3.
setup: Gracilis is superficial and thin — landmark-guided injection is often adequate, but USG can confirm you are in gracilis and not the deeper adductor longus.
The muscle is a thin strap — use low volume to avoid diffusion into adjacent adductors.
The saphenous nerve and great saphenous vein run in the medial thigh — they are anterior to gracilis but should be identified if using US.
Patient position: supine with the leg slightly abducted.

ultrasound.orientation: Transverse across the proximal medial thigh
viewSteps: Place the probe transversely on the proximal medial thigh with the hip abducted.
Gracilis appears as a thin, flat hypoechoic muscle strap on the most medial and superficial aspect of the thigh, directly under the subcutaneous tissue.
Deep to gracilis, the adductor longus is visible as a larger, thicker hypoechoic muscle.
The sartorius is visible anterolaterally — do not confuse the two (sartorius is more lateral and anterior).
To confirm: ask the patient to adduct the hip — gracilis will contract and thicken on real-time US.
safetyNotes: The saphenous nerve and great saphenous vein run in the subsartorial canal anterior to gracilis — identify them if visible and avoid.
Stay within the thin gracilis belly — deep penetration enters adductor longus.
The obturator nerve branches are deep to gracilis in the adductor compartment.

dosageNote: Thin muscle — conservative dosing to avoid spread to adjacent adductors.
probePlacementHint: Patient supine, frog-leg position. Place probe transversely on proximal medial thigh. Photo from medial view showing probe on inner thigh.
pearls: The only adductor that crosses both hip and knee — contributes to both scissoring AND knee flexion
Standard target in adductor injection sets alongside longus and magnus — don't forget it
Very thin and superficial — easy to over-penetrate into deeper adductors; use short needle and minimal depth
Flexes both at the hip and knee; primarily active in initial hip flexion.
Rarely treated individually — must be considered when treating adductor-group spasm since gracilis contributes to the adduction pattern.
supplies: 25-27G needle (1.5 inch for superficial, 2-3 inch for deep)
dangerZones: Going too deep risks hitting adductor magnus.
positionLabel: Supine · frog-leg (hip abducted & externally rotated)

name: Rectus Femoris
landmarks: AIIS (Anterior Inferior Iliac Spine — palpate 2 cm below the ASIS; this deep bony point is the origin of the rectus femoris direct head)
Superior Pole of Patella (palpate the top of the kneecap — the rectus femoris tendon inserts here as part of the quadriceps tendon)
Anterior inferior iliac spine (AIIS) — straight head of origin.
Superior border of the acetabulum — reflected (posterior) head of origin.
Patella — insertion via the patellar ligament to the tibial tuberosity.
Anchor: middle of the muscle belly, on a line from ASIS/AIIS to the patella.
placement: Position the patient supine with the knee extended and the thigh relaxed.
Identify the mid-thigh by measuring halfway between the ASIS and the superior pole of the patella.
The rectus femoris is the most superficial and central muscle of the anterior thigh at this level.
Palpate the muscle belly — ask the patient to extend the knee against resistance to confirm.
Insert the needle perpendicular to the skin into the bulk of the muscle belly at mid-thigh.
Advance 1-2 cm into the muscle, staying superficial to the Vastus Intermedius below.
Aspirate before injecting. Distribute the dose across 2 sites within the muscle belly if using higher doses.
Injection site: middle of the muscle belly, midway between the ASIS and the proximal patella.
Sites: 1-3.
setup: USG is recommended to distinguish the fascial septum between Rectus Femoris and the underlying Vastus Intermedius.
The Rectus Femoris is the only biarticular quadriceps muscle — it contributes to stiff-knee gait when spastic.
Surface anatomy is usually sufficient for identification, but USG helps confirm depth.
Have the patient extend the knee against resistance to identify the muscle bulk before marking.
Patient position: supine.

ultrasound.orientation: Transverse across the anterior mid-thigh
viewSteps: Identify subcutaneous fat and the superficial fascia (fascia lata) as the most superficial hyperechoic layers.
The Rectus Femoris appears as a prominent oval hypoechoic muscle belly in the center of the anterior thigh, with a bright fascial envelope.
On either side, the Vastus Lateralis (lateral) and Vastus Medialis (medial) are visible as large hypoechoic muscles.
Deep to the Rectus Femoris, a bright hyperechoic fascial plane separates it from the Vastus Intermedius.
The Vastus Intermedius lies directly on the hyperechoic cortex of the femoral shaft.
safetyNotes: The femoral nerve, artery, and vein lie in the femoral triangle (medial proximal thigh) — avoid the proximal medial approach.
The descending branch of the lateral circumflex femoral artery runs between the rectus femoris and vastus lateralis — use color Doppler.
Ensure the injection is superficial to the fascial plane separating the RF from the Vastus Intermedius.

probePlacementHint: Patient supine, knee extended. Place probe transversely on anterior mid-thigh. Photo from lateral view showing probe across anterior thigh.
pearls: The only quad that crosses the hip — contributes to both stiff knee gait AND hip flexion
Key target for stiff-knee gait pattern in stroke and TBI
Superficial and easy to identify — one of the most straightforward injections
The different components of quadriceps femoris must always be viewed as a whole — rectus femoris acts on TWO joints (hip flexion + knee extension) simultaneously.
Rectus femoris is the primary quadriceps contributor to stiff-knee gait in hemiparetic patients.
supplies: 25-27G needle (1.5 inch for superficial, 2-3 inch for deep)
dosageNote: Primary stiff-knee gait target. 1-2 sites in proximal-mid muscle belly.
dangerZones: The femoral nerve, artery, and vein lie in the femoral triangle (medial proximal thigh) — avoid the proximal medial approach.
The descending branch of the lateral circumflex femoral artery runs between the rectus femoris and vastus lateralis — use color Doppler.
positionLabel: Supine · knee extended, thigh relaxed

name: Vastus Lateralis
landmarks: Greater Trochanter (palpate the bony prominence on the lateral hip — the VL originates from the intertrochanteric line and lateral femur distal to this)
Lateral Condyle of Femur (palpate the bony prominence on the lateral knee — the VL inserts via the quadriceps tendon and lateral retinaculum)
IT Band (palpate the taut band on the lateral thigh — the VL lies deep/anterior to this fascial structure)
Greater trochanter and lateral lip of the linea aspera (origin).
Patella — lateral portion of the patellar retinaculum (insertion).
Anchor: middle-to-distal portion of the muscle belly, approximately 10-11 cm proximal to the superolateral patella.
placement: Position the patient supine or in lateral decubitus with the affected side up.
Identify the mid-to-distal lateral thigh (approximately the middle third of the femur length).
Palpate the IT band as a taut fascial band on the lateral thigh.
The injection target is deep and anterior to the IT band, into the muscle belly pressed against the femur.
Insert the needle through the IT band, angling slightly anteriorly to enter the VL muscle belly.
Advance 2-3 cm into the muscle substance until you feel the firm muscle against bone.
Avoid injecting into the IT band itself — it is a fascial structure and toxin will not be effective there.
Aspirate before injecting. Use multiple injection sites (2-3) along the length of the muscle for adequate coverage.
Injection site: middle and distal portion of the muscle belly, on the lateral thigh.
Sites: 1-3, usually 1-2.
setup: Multiple injection sites are often needed along the length of the femur for this large muscle.
Ensure the needle passes through the IT band into actual muscle tissue.
The VL is a common intramuscular injection site (vaccinations) — familiarity with the anatomy is helpful.
USG can confirm that the needle is in muscle tissue and not in the IT band or subcutaneous fat.
Patient position: supine or lateral decubitus with the affected side up.

ultrasound.orientation: Transverse across the lateral mid-thigh
viewSteps: Identify subcutaneous fat and the fascia lata (including the IT band component) as hyperechoic superficial layers.
The Vastus Lateralis appears as a large hypoechoic muscle deep to the IT band, wrapping around the lateral femur.
The hyperechoic cortex of the femoral shaft is visible deep to the VL as a bright curved line with posterior shadowing.
Medially, the Vastus Intermedius and Rectus Femoris may be visible separated by fascial planes.
safetyNotes: The descending branch of the lateral circumflex femoral artery runs in the intermuscular septum between VL and RF — use color Doppler.
Perforating branches of the profunda femoris artery may cross the field — aspirate before injecting.
The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve is more proximal and superficial — it is at risk only with very proximal injections.

probePlacementHint: Patient supine or lateral. Place probe transversely on lateral mid-thigh. Photo from lateral view showing probe on outer thigh.
pearls: Often contributes to knee extension spasticity more than rectus femoris
Large muscle belly — may need multiple injection points for adequate distribution
Largest component of the quadriceps — the easiest vastus to inject.
supplies: 25-27G needle (1.5 inch for superficial, 2-3 inch for deep)
dangerZones: Safe injection zone is the lateral thigh — away from major neurovascular structures
Going too medial or too distal risks the needle rotating into rectus femoris or infiltrating into the femur.
positionLabel: Supine or lateral decubitus · affected side up

name: Vastus Medialis
landmarks: Adductor Tubercle (palpate the bony prominence on the medial femoral condyle — the VMO fibers originate from the adductor magnus tendon near here)
Patella (palpate the kneecap — the VMO inserts on its superomedial border with an oblique fiber orientation)
Sartorius (palpate the strap-like muscle crossing the medial thigh obliquely — the VMO lies deep and lateral to its distal portion)
Patella — vastus medialis inserts via its medial portion into the medial patellar retinaculum.
Medial intermuscular septum / medial supracondylar ridge of the femur (origin).
Anchor: approximately 7-8 cm (4 fingers) proximal to a line drawn from the superior patella to the medial epicondyle of the femur.
placement: Position the patient supine with the knee extended and the thigh relaxed.
Identify the distal third of the medial thigh — the VMO is prominent here.
Palpate the characteristic 'teardrop' shape of the VMO just proximal and medial to the patella.
Ask the patient to extend the knee against resistance — the VMO will contract visibly and palpably.
Insert the needle perpendicular to the skin into the bulk of the VMO muscle belly.
Advance 1-2 cm into the muscle substance.
Aspirate before injecting. A single injection site in the mid-belly is usually sufficient.
Injection site: distal portion of the muscle belly, 7-8 cm (4 fingers) proximal to the patella on the medial side.
Sites: 1-3.
Injection depth: 15-30 mm.
setup: USG is optional but helpful to avoid the adductor canal neurovascular bundle, which lies deep to the Sartorius.
The VMO is superficial and easily identified by palpation in most patients.
Be aware that the saphenous nerve and descending genicular artery run in the adductor canal deep and medial to the VMO.
This injection is rarely performed in isolation — usually part of a broader quadriceps toxin strategy.
Patient position: supine with the leg extended.
US guidance recommended — femoral vessels run in the anteromedial thigh; going too medial risks neurovascular injection.

ultrasound.orientation: Transverse across the distal medial thigh, just proximal to the patella
viewSteps: Identify subcutaneous tissue and the superficial fascia as hyperechoic layers.
The Sartorius appears as a thin, strap-like hypoechoic muscle superficially on the medial side.
Deep and lateral to the Sartorius, the Vastus Medialis appears as a large teardrop-shaped hypoechoic muscle with oblique fiber orientation.
Deep to the Sartorius and medial to the VMO, identify the adductor canal — the femoral artery appears as an anechoic pulsatile circle with color Doppler flow.
The hyperechoic cortex of the distal femur provides the deep bony landmark.
safetyNotes: The saphenous nerve and descending genicular artery travel in the adductor canal deep to the Sartorius — do not inject too medially or deeply.
The femoral artery transitions to the popliteal artery through the adductor hiatus in this region — use color Doppler.
The medial superior genicular artery runs near the distal VMO — aspirate before injection.

probePlacementHint: Patient supine, knee extended. Place probe transversely on distal medial thigh, just above patella (VMO area). Photo showing probe on medial knee/thigh junction.
pearls: VMO dysfunction contributes to patellar tracking issues in spastic patients
Inject at the distal bulge (VMO) — most identifiable part
Rarely injected in isolation — usually part of a multi-muscle quad program
Works with the other vasti to stabilize the knee — they must be considered together.
supplies: 25-27G needle (1.5 inch for superficial, 2-3 inch for deep)
dosageNote: Use cautiously — weakening VMO can destabilize the patella.
dangerZones: Going too medial risks injection into the femoral neurovascular bundle.
positionLabel: Supine · knee extended, thigh relaxed

name: Vastus Intermedius
landmarks: Anterior Femur (not directly palpable — lies deep to the rectus femoris; approximate by palpating the mid-anterior thigh)
Deep to Rectus Femoris (the VI is only accessible by passing through or around the RF — the fascial septum between them is the key landmark)
Anterior shaft of the femur (origin — upper two-thirds).
Patella — insertion via the patellar ligament to the tibial tuberosity.
Anchor: middle of a line between the ASIS and the proximal patella.
placement: Position the patient supine with the knee extended and the thigh relaxed.
Identify the proximal-to-mid anterior thigh (the VI belly is largest in the proximal third).
Palpate the Rectus Femoris muscle belly — the Vastus Intermedius lies directly deep to it.
Insert the needle perpendicular to the skin through the center of the Rectus Femoris.
Advance through the RF (typically 1-2 cm) until you feel a subtle 'pop' through the fascial septum separating the two muscles.
Continue advancing into the VI muscle belly, which sits directly on the femoral shaft (total depth approximately 2-4 cm).
Stop before contacting the periosteum of the femur.
Aspirate before injecting. USG confirmation of needle position is mandatory.
Injection site: middle of the anterior thigh, deep to rectus femoris, on the line from ASIS to patella.
Sites: 1-2.
Injection depth: 3-5 cm (deep to rectus femoris).
setup: USG is MANDATORY to effectively distinguish the fascial plane between Rectus Femoris and Vastus Intermedius.
An in-plane needle approach under US allows real-time visualization of the needle crossing the fascial septum.
The VI is the deepest quadriceps muscle and cannot be reliably targeted by palpation alone.
This injection is often performed in conjunction with RF injection — plan your dose distribution accordingly.
Patient position: supine with the leg extended.
US guidance essential — vastus intermedius cannot be palpated and cannot be reliably differentiated from the other vasti without imaging.

ultrasound.orientation: Transverse across the anterior proximal-to-mid thigh

The Rectus Femoris appears as the superficial oval hypoechoic muscle in the center of the field.
Deep to the RF, identify the bright hyperechoic fascial septum — this is your target plane to cross.

The hyperechoic cortex of the femoral shaft lies immediately deep to the VI — this is your depth limit.
safetyNotes: The descending branch of the lateral circumflex femoral artery runs laterally between the muscles — use color Doppler before inserting.
Do not advance the needle to the periosteum of the femur, which causes pain and is not the target.

pearls: Deepest of the quadriceps — requires longer needle and confident US identification
Lies directly on the femur — use the femur as your deep landmark on US
Often co-injected when other quads alone don't adequately reduce extension tone

Deep to rectus femoris; pass the needle through rectus to reach it.

name: Biceps Femoris
landmarks: Ischial Tuberosity (palpate the large bony prominence deep in the inferior gluteal fold — the long head of the biceps femoris originates here, sharing a conjoined tendon with the semitendinosus)
Fibular Head (palpate the small bony prominence on the lateral aspect of the proximal leg just below the knee — the biceps femoris tendon inserts here and is easily palpable as a taut cord)

Lateral Hamstring Tendon (with the knee flexed to 90 degrees, palpate the prominent tendon on the posterolateral aspect of the knee running toward the fibular head — this defines the lateral border of the popliteal fossa)
Long head: ischial tuberosity (origin). Anchor the injection at the middle of a line between the ischial tuberosity and the popliteal fossa (approximately 4 fingers).
Short head: linea aspera (origin). Anchor approximately 2 cm above the popliteal cavity, superficial to the head of the fibula.
Head of the fibula (insertion) — palpable lateral bony prominence behind the knee.
placement: Position the patient prone with the knee slightly flexed over a pillow or bolster.
Identify the biceps femoris — it is the lateral hamstring muscle; have the patient flex the knee against resistance to make the muscle belly and distal tendon prominent.
The injection site for the long head is at the junction of the proximal and middle thirds of the posterior thigh on the lateral side.
Insert the needle perpendicular to the skin into the lateral muscle belly of the posterior thigh.
Advance approximately 1.5-3 cm depending on subcutaneous tissue thickness — the biceps femoris long head is relatively superficial in the lateral posterior thigh.

Aspirate before injecting. Distribute the dose across 2 sites within the long head muscle belly. If the short head is also targeted, inject separately at the distal third of the lateral posterior thigh.
Long head injection: middle of the line between ischial tuberosity and popliteal cavity, approximately 4 fingers distal to the ischial tuberosity. Sites: 1-3.
Short head injection: 2 cm above the popliteal cavity, superficial to the fibular head, medial or lateral to the short-head belly. Sites: 1-2.
setup: USG is recommended to differentiate the long head from the short head and to identify the sciatic nerve.
Have the patient flex the knee against resistance to clearly delineate the biceps femoris from the medial hamstrings (semimembranosus and semitendinosus).
The sciatic nerve (or its divisions: tibial and common peroneal nerves) runs medial and deep to the biceps femoris in the posterior thigh — confirm its position before injecting.
The common peroneal nerve wraps around the fibular head immediately deep to the biceps femoris tendon distally — do not inject near the distal tendon insertion.
Patient position: prone.

ultrasound.probe: High-frequency linear (10-15 MHz) or low-frequency curvilinear (5-8 MHz) for deeper targets
ultrasound.orientation: Transverse across the lateral posterior thigh at the junction of the proximal and middle thirds
viewSteps: Identify subcutaneous fat and the deep fascia (fascia lata) as the superficial layers.
The Biceps Femoris Long Head appears as a large hypoechoic muscle belly in the lateral posterior thigh, superficial to the short head.
Deep and slightly medial, identify the Biceps Femoris Short Head as a smaller hypoechoic muscle arising from the linea aspera of the femur.
Medial to the biceps femoris, identify the Semitendinosus (with its characteristic round tendon) and the Semimembranosus (broader and deeper).
Between the medial and lateral hamstrings, identify the sciatic nerve as a hyperechoic oval or honeycomb structure — it lies deep in the fascial plane.
The femur appears as a hyperechoic line with acoustic shadowing in the deep field.
safetyNotes: The sciatic nerve courses medial and deep to the biceps femoris long head — always identify it with ultrasound before injecting.
The common peroneal nerve separates from the tibial nerve in the distal thigh and runs along the medial border of the biceps femoris tendon — avoid the distal tendon region.
The popliteal artery and vein lie deep in the popliteal fossa medially — do not inject too medially or too deeply in the distal thigh.
Differentiate the long head (superficial, originates from ischial tuberosity) from the short head (deep, originates from the femur) as they may require separate targeting.

probePlacementHint: Patient prone, knee flexed over pillow. Place probe transversely on lateral posterior thigh at junction of proximal and middle thirds. Photo from behind showing probe on posterolateral thigh.
pearls: Lateral hamstring — key target for lateral knee flexion patterns
Common peroneal nerve branches from sciatic near the biceps femoris tendon — identify on US
Long and short heads may need separate injection points

Can rotate the flexed knee laterally — its action is distinct from semitendinosus and semimembranosus.

dangerZones: Going too medial (from either head) risks penetrating semitendinosus.
positionLabel: Prone · knee slightly flexed (pillow/bolster)

name: Semitendinosus
landmarks: Ischial Tuberosity (palpate the bony prominence at the base of the buttock with the hip flexed — the semitendinosus shares a common origin tendon with the biceps femoris here)
Medial Tibial Condyle (palpate the medial proximal tibia — the semitendinosus inserts on the anteromedial surface as part of the pes anserinus)
Ischial tuberosity (origin, shared with biceps femoris long head).
Medial tibial surface (pes anserinus insertion).
Anchor: middle of the posteromedial thigh, on a line between ischial tuberosity and the pes anserinus.
placement: Position the patient prone with the knee slightly flexed (place a pillow under the ankle).
Identify the mid-thigh on the directly posterior surface.
Ask the patient to flex the knee against resistance — palpate the medial hamstring group.
The Semitendinosus is the superficial medial hamstring; it often has a distinct raphe (tendinous inscription) in the mid-belly.
Palpate the round muscle belly — it becomes a long, cord-like tendon in the distal third.
Insert the needle perpendicular to the skin into the mid-belly of the muscle (proximal to the tendinous portion).
Advance 1-2 cm into the muscle substance — it is relatively superficial.
Aspirate before injecting.
Injection site: middle of the muscle belly.
Sites: 1-3, usually 1-2.
Injection depth: 15-30 mm.
setup: The semitendinosus is easily palpable in most patients.
Confirm the correct muscle by having the patient flex the knee against resistance — feel for the superficial medial cord.
Inject into the fleshy belly, not the distal tendon (which begins roughly at the junction of the middle and distal thirds).
USG is generally not required but can confirm you are in the correct muscle.
Patient position: prone.

ultrasound.orientation: Transverse across the posterior mid-thigh
viewSteps: Identify subcutaneous tissue and the deep fascia superficially.
The Semitendinosus appears as a round or oval hypoechoic muscle belly in the medial posterior thigh — it is the most superficial of the medial hamstrings.

Deep to the Semitendinosus, the broader Semimembranosus is visible as a flatter hypoechoic structure.
safetyNotes: The sciatic nerve runs laterally in the posterior thigh — it is generally safe with a medial injection approach.
The posterior femoral cutaneous nerve runs superficially in the midline — avoid the most superficial subcutaneous plane.
Distally, the popliteal vessels are at risk — do not inject in the distal third of the thigh.

probePlacementHint: Patient prone, knee slightly flexed. Place probe transversely on posterior mid-thigh. Photo from behind showing probe on posterior thigh, medial side.
pearls: Round tendon easily palpated posteromedially — the muscle belly is proximal
Often has a ropy, cord-like tendon that's palpable behind the knee
Co-injection with semimembranosus gives better results than either alone for hamstring spasticity
Long tendon of insertion can be palpated in the belly of the muscle — use it to orient during injection.
Contraction affects lumbar lordosis indirectly; works antagonistically to hip flexors.
supplies: 25-27G needle (1.5 inch for superficial, 2-3 inch for deep)
dangerZones: The sciatic nerve runs laterally in the posterior thigh — it is generally safe with a medial injection approach.
The posterior femoral cutaneous nerve runs superficially in the midline — avoid the most superficial subcutaneous plane.
Distally, the popliteal vessels are at risk — do not inject in the distal third of the thigh.
positionLabel: Prone · knee slightly flexed (pillow/bolster)

name: Semimembranosus
landmarks: Ischial Tuberosity (palpate the bony prominence at the base of the buttock with the hip flexed — the semimembranosus originates here, lateral to the semitendinosus origin)
Medial Tibial Condyle (palpate the broad bony prominence on the medial proximal tibia — the semimembranosus inserts on its posterior surface)
Ischial tuberosity (origin).
Posterior aspect of the medial tibial condyle (insertion).
Anchor: distal portion of the posterior thigh, at the lateral margin of the semimembranosus tendon as it approaches the knee.
placement: Position the patient prone with the knee slightly flexed (place a pillow under the ankle).
Identify the mid-thigh to distal thigh on the posterior-medial aspect.
Ask the patient to flex the knee against resistance — palpate the medial hamstrings.
The Semitendinosus is the superficial medial hamstring with a prominent tendon distally; the Semimembranosus is deep to it.
Approach from the medial side of the thigh to access the semimembranosus belly.
Insert the needle from the medial aspect, angling slightly posteriorly and laterally to pass deep to the Semitendinosus.
Advance 2-3 cm to reach the semimembranosus muscle belly.
Aspirate before injecting. Confirm placement with ultrasound.
Injection site: distal portion of the posterior-medial thigh.
Sites: 1-3, usually 1-2.
setup: USG is helpful to distinguish the semimembranosus from the more superficial semitendinosus.
The semimembranosus has a broad, flat 'membranous' appearance on ultrasound, in contrast to the round semitendinosus.
Have the patient flex the knee against resistance to identify the hamstring group.
The sciatic nerve runs laterally in the posterior thigh — it is generally not at risk with a medial approach.
Patient position: prone.
US guidance recommended — the three hamstring muscles are difficult to differentiate by palpation alone.

ultrasound.orientation: Transverse across the posterior medial thigh at mid-to-distal level
viewSteps: Identify subcutaneous tissue and the deep fascia as superficial hyperechoic layers.
The Semitendinosus appears as a round or oval hypoechoic muscle belly superficially (or its hyperechoic tendon distally).
Deep to the Semitendinosus, the Semimembranosus appears as a broader, flatter hypoechoic muscle with a characteristic 'membranous' aponeurosis.

probePlacementHint: Patient prone, knee slightly flexed. Place probe transversely on posterior medial thigh at mid-to-distal level. Photo from behind showing probe on posteromedial thigh.
pearls: Broader, flatter muscle — differentiate from semitendinosus by its deeper position and membranous aponeurosis on ultrasound.
Key hamstring for medial knee flexion contracture patterns
Can be absent or fused with semitendinosus — if expected anatomy is not seen, look for the fused variant.
The three hamstring muscles are difficult to differentiate from one another; treat them with awareness of their combined action.

dangerZones: Sciatic nerve runs in the posterior thigh — always identify it before injecting
positionLabel: Prone · knee slightly flexed (pillow/bolster)

name: Gastrocnemius (Medial)
landmarks: Medial Femoral Condyle (palpate the bony prominence on the medial knee — the medial gastrocnemius head originates from its posterior surface)
Popliteal Fossa (palpate the diamond-shaped depression behind the knee — the gastrocnemius heads form the distal borders of this fossa)
Popliteal crease — palpable behind the knee, forms the proximal boundary of the gastroc.
Medial femoral condyle (medial head origin).
Anchor: approximately 4 fingers (8-10 cm) distal to the popliteal crease, in the muscle belly of the medial head.
placement: Position the patient prone with the feet hanging off the edge of the bed.
Identify the proximal third of the posterior calf — this is where the medial gastrocnemius belly is largest.
Palpate the large medial muscle belly — ask the patient to plantarflex the ankle against resistance to confirm.
The injection site is 2-3 cm distal to the popliteal crease, on the medial side of the calf midline.
Insert the needle perpendicular to the skin into the bulk of the medial gastrocnemius belly.
Advance 1-2 cm into the muscle — the gastrocnemius is superficial.
Aspirate before injecting. Distribute the dose across 2 sites within the medial belly if using higher doses.
Injection site: muscle belly of both medial and lateral heads, approximately 4 fingers (8-10 cm) distal to the popliteal crease.
Sites: 1-3 per head (medial and lateral), usually 2 sites.
Injection depth: 2-4 cm, depending on muscle thickness.

The medial head is larger than the lateral head — it is the primary contributor to equinus in most patients.
Prone positioning with feet off the table edge allows easy access and palpation.
This is one of the most commonly injected muscles in spasticity management — practice good technique here.
Patient position: prone, feet hanging over the edge of the table to relax the calf.

ultrasound.orientation: Transverse across the proximal medial posterior calf, 2-3 cm distal to the popliteal crease
viewSteps: Identify subcutaneous fat and the superficial fascia.
The medial Gastrocnemius appears as a large, thick hypoechoic muscle with a pennate fiber pattern and bright fascial borders.

Between the two Gastrocnemius heads in the midline, the sural nerve and small saphenous vein may be visible.

The popliteal artery and tibial nerve lie deep in the proximal popliteal fossa — do not inject too proximally or deeply.
The medial sural cutaneous nerve branches from the tibial nerve — it is superficial to the gastrocnemius fascia.

probePlacementHint: Patient prone, feet off bed edge. Place probe transversely on proximal medial calf, 2-3 cm below popliteal crease. Photo from behind showing probe on medial proximal calf.

Inject proximal — the muscle belly is short and becomes tendinous quickly

name: Gastrocnemius (Lateral)
landmarks: Lateral Femoral Condyle (palpate the bony prominence on the lateral knee — the lateral gastrocnemius head originates from its posterior surface)
Fibular Head (palpate the small bony knob on the proximal lateral leg, just distal to the knee — the common peroneal nerve wraps around it)
Popliteal crease — palpable behind the knee.
Lateral femoral condyle (lateral head origin).
Anchor: approximately 4 fingers (8-10 cm) distal to the popliteal crease, in the muscle belly of the lateral head.

Identify the proximal third of the posterior calf on the lateral side.
Palpate the lateral gastrocnemius belly — it is smaller than the medial head.

The injection site is in the center of the lateral gastrocnemius belly, 2-3 cm distal to the popliteal crease, well medial to the fibular head. Maintain at least 2 cm of clearance from the fibular head to avoid the common peroneal nerve.
Insert the needle perpendicular to the skin into the lateral muscle belly.
Advance 1-1.5 cm into the muscle substance.
Aspirate before injecting.
Injection site: muscle belly of the lateral head, approximately 4 fingers (8-10 cm) distal to the popliteal crease.
Sites: 1-3 per head.
Injection depth: 2-4 cm, depending on muscle thickness.
setup: The lateral head is usually smaller in bulk than the medial head.
Avoid the Common Peroneal Nerve, which wraps around the fibular head — stay medial to the fibular head.
This injection is often combined with the medial gastrocnemius injection for equinus management.
USG can help distinguish the lateral gastrocnemius from the underlying soleus and plantaris.
Patient position: prone, feet hanging over the edge of the table.
Common peroneal nerve runs lateral to the gastroc at the fibular head — stay in the muscle belly, do not go too lateral.

ultrasound.orientation: Transverse across the proximal lateral posterior calf, 2-3 cm distal to the popliteal crease

The lateral Gastrocnemius appears as a hypoechoic muscle belly — it is typically thinner and narrower than the medial head.

The popliteal vessels are deep and proximal — do not inject too deeply in the proximal calf.

probePlacementHint: Patient prone, feet off bed edge. Place probe transversely on proximal lateral calf, 2-3 cm below popliteal crease. Photo from behind showing probe on lateral proximal calf.
pearls: Smaller than medial head — use lower doses
Often co-injected with medial gastroc and soleus for equinus pattern
The lateral head is usually smaller and contributes less to equinus than the medial head.
supplies: 25-27G needle (1.5 inch for superficial, 2-3 inch for deep)
dangerZones: Common peroneal nerve runs nearby at the fibular neck — stay distal and medial
Going too deep risks the soleus.

name: Soleus (Medial)
landmarks: Medial Border of Tibia (palpate the sharp subcutaneous border of the tibia on the medial leg — the soleus originates from the posterior tibial surface just behind this edge)
Deep to Gastrocnemius (the soleus lies entirely deep to the gastrocnemius in the proximal calf — it extends more distally and is accessible where the gastrocnemius tapers)
Soleal line of the tibia and upper third of the posterior fibula (origin).
Calcaneal tuberosity via the Achilles tendon (insertion).
Middle-to-distal posterior calf — soleus is deep to gastrocnemius.

Palpate the medial border of the tibia in the mid-to-distal calf.
Move your palpating finger 1-2 cm posterior to the tibial border — this is where the soleus is accessible.
The injection site is distal to the bulk of the medial gastrocnemius belly (approximately mid-calf level).
Insert the needle perpendicular to the skin, directed slightly laterally and posteriorly.
Advance 2-3 cm to pass deep to the Gastrocnemius and enter the Soleus muscle belly.
Under ultrasound, confirm the needle tip has crossed the fascial plane between the two muscles.
Aspirate before injecting. Distribute the dose across 2 sites.
Injection site: middle-to-distal posterior calf, deep to the gastroc.
Sites: 2-4.
setup: USG is highly recommended to distinguish the fascial plane between Gastrocnemius (superficial) and Soleus (deep).
The soleus is a large muscle that extends more distally than the gastrocnemius — it is best accessed in the mid-to-distal calf.
An in-plane needle approach allows real-time visualization of the needle crossing into the soleus.
The posterior tibial neurovascular bundle runs deep to the soleus — do not advance too deeply.
Patient position: prone.
US guidance recommended — soleus lies deep to gastroc and must be distinguished from it.

ultrasound.orientation: Transverse across the medial mid-calf, 1-2 cm posterior to the tibial border
viewSteps: Identify subcutaneous tissue and superficial fascia.
The Gastrocnemius (or its aponeurosis distally) appears as a superficial hypoechoic layer with a bright fascial border.
Deep to the Gastrocnemius, a bright hyperechoic fascial septum marks the boundary with the Soleus.
The Soleus appears as a large hypoechoic muscle with a complex multipennate fiber architecture, distinctly different from the Gastrocnemius.
Deep to the Soleus, the posterior tibial vessels and tibial nerve may be visible — these are your deep boundary.

The saphenous vein and nerve run subcutaneously along the medial leg — avoid very superficial injury.
Peroneal vessels may be encountered laterally if the needle is directed too far lateral.

probePlacementHint: Patient prone, feet off edge. Place probe transversely on medial mid-calf, just posterior to tibial border. Photo from behind/medial showing probe on mid-calf.
pearls: Deep to gastrocnemius — must angle the needle past gastroc on US
Key differentiator: gastroc crosses the knee, soleus doesn't. Test with knee flexed vs extended
If equinus persists with knee flexed, soleus is the primary contributor
Part of the triceps surae with gastrocnemius and plantaris — full calf plantarflexion is only controlled when all three are addressed.
Critical muscle for equinus not responsive to gastroc-only injection.
supplies: 25-27G needle (1.5 inch for superficial, 2-3 inch for deep)
dangerZones: The posterior tibial artery and tibial nerve run deep to the soleus in the deep posterior compartment — do not advance the needle through the soleus.
The saphenous vein and nerve run subcutaneously along the medial leg — avoid very superficial injury.
Peroneal vessels may be encountered laterally if the needle is directed too far lateral.

name: Soleus (Lateral)
landmarks: Fibula (palpate the lateral leg bone — the soleus originates from the posterior surface of the proximal fibular head and shaft)
Lateral Border of Gastrocnemius (palpate the lateral gastrocnemius belly — the lateral soleus is accessible just lateral/anterior to where the gastrocnemius tapers)

Insert the needle perpendicular to the skin into this lateral soleus bulge at mid-calf level.
Advance 1-2 cm into the muscle belly.
Aspirate before injecting. Multiple distal injection sites may be used along the length of the muscle.
setup: Multiple distal injection sites may be needed to adequately address spasticity throughout this large muscle.
The lateral approach avoids the posterior tibial neurovascular bundle, which runs more medially.
USG can confirm needle placement within the soleus and not in the gastrocnemius or peroneal muscles.
The soleus is primarily a slow-twitch postural muscle — it often requires higher doses than the gastrocnemius.

ultrasound.orientation: Transverse across the lateral mid-calf
viewSteps: Identify subcutaneous tissue and superficial fascia.
The lateral Gastrocnemius (or its aponeurosis) appears as a superficial hypoechoic layer, tapering distally.
Deep and lateral, the Soleus appears as a broad hypoechoic muscle with a multipennate pattern.
The fibula appears as a bright hyperechoic cortical line laterally with posterior acoustic shadowing.
safetyNotes: The peroneal artery runs between the soleus and tibialis posterior in the deep compartment — use color Doppler.
The sural nerve runs superficially in the subcutaneous tissue of the posterior calf — avoid very superficial injection.
The common peroneal nerve wraps around the proximal fibula — stay distal to the fibular head.

probePlacementHint: Patient prone, feet off edge. Place probe transversely on lateral mid-calf. Photo from behind showing probe on lateral mid-calf.
pearls: Less commonly injected than medial soleus but important for varus component
Smaller volume than medial — adjust dosing accordingly

positionLabel: Prone · feet hanging off the edge of the bed

name: Tibialis Posterior
landmarks: Medial Tibial Border (palpate the sharp subcutaneous tibial edge — the tibialis posterior lies on the posterior surface of the interosseous membrane, deep to the superficial posterior compartment muscles)
Fibular Head (palpate the bony knob on the proximal lateral leg — helps orient the interosseous membrane between tibia and fibula)
Intermalleolar Line (draw an imaginary line between the medial and lateral malleoli — the midpoint of the leg between the fibular head and this line approximates the mid-belly)
Lateral part of the posterior tibia, interosseous membrane, proximal posterior fibula (origin).
Navicular tuberosity (primary insertion) — palpable medial-plantar foot bony prominence.
Tibialis posterior is the deepest of the posterior-compartment muscles — below soleus, between tibia and fibula.
placement: Position the patient prone or supine with the leg externally rotated.
Identify the midpoint between the fibular head and the intermalleolar line on the medial leg.
Approach from the medial side of the leg, posterior to the medial tibial border.
Insert the needle directed posterolaterally, sliding along the posterior aspect of the tibia.
Advance through the superficial posterior compartment muscles (Gastrocnemius/Soleus) toward the interosseous membrane.
The tibialis posterior lies directly on the interosseous membrane — it is the deepest muscle in this compartment.
Typical depth is 3-5 cm depending on body habitus — USG confirms placement.
Aspirate before injecting. Confirm the needle is in the tibialis posterior and not in overlying muscles.
Injection site: middle-to-distal posterior leg, deep to soleus and flexor digitorum longus.
Sites: 1-3.
setup: USG is MANDATORY — high risk of posterior tibial artery and tibial nerve injury.
The tibialis posterior is the deepest muscle in the deep posterior compartment.
Use an in-plane needle approach for continuous visualization during this deep injection.
Have the patient invert the foot against resistance to confirm the muscle on ultrasound — this is the strongest foot invertor.
Patient position: prone or supine with the leg externally rotated.
US guidance strongly recommended — tibialis posterior is deep; needle must pass through overlying muscles.

ultrasound.probe: High-frequency linear (10-15 MHz) in thin patients; lower-frequency linear (6-9 MHz) or curvilinear (5-8 MHz) is often required in average/larger patients due to muscle depth (3-5+ cm)
ultrasound.orientation: Transverse across the medial mid-leg, posterior to the tibial border

Deep to the Soleus, the posterior tibial vessels (pulsatile anechoic circles) and tibial nerve (hyperechoic honeycomb) are visible in the deep posterior compartment.
The Tibialis Posterior appears as a hypoechoic muscle belly lying directly on the hyperechoic interosseous membrane, deep to the neurovascular bundle.
The bright cortical lines of the tibia (medially) and fibula (laterally) frame the compartment — the interosseous membrane connects them.
